knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional support functions as convex supremal objective models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty. Its support function is the extended-real function
\[
\sigma_C(x):=\sup_{c\in C}\langle c,x\rangle,
\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
The function \(\sigma_C\) is convex and positively homogeneous. Moreover, \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}C}\), so the model depends only on the closed convex hull of \(C\). If \(C\) is compact, the supremum is finite and attained for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A support function is the supremum of linear forms indexed by a set; it is convex, positively homogeneous, and determined by the set’s closed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C(x)=\sup_{c\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\) and \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}C}\).

source_refs.locator: 5.3 Value Functions Associated with Convex Functions p. 268

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3 Value Functions Associated with Convex Functions p. 268

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Supremum Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity and lower semicontinuity inherited by arbitrary pointwise suprema.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(T\neq\varnothing\), and let \(f_t:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex for every \(t\in T\). Define
\[
f(x):=\sup_{t\in T}f_t(x).
\]
Then \(f\) is convex, possibly identically \(+\infty\). If every \(f_t\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(f\) is lower semicontinuous because
\[
\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_{t\in T}\operatorname{epi}f_t.
\]
No attainment of the supremum by an index \(t\) is implied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrary pointwise supremum of convex functions is convex, and it is lower semicontinuous when every constituent is lower semicontinuous; a maximizing index need not exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=\sup_{t\in T}f_t\) is convex, and it is lower semicontinuous if all \(f_t\) are lower semicontinuous.

children.title: Parametric Max-Value Models
children.top_down_role: Max-value models separated by attainment and stability of their parameterized maximizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Parameter Max-Value Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite maxima of parameterized convex component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), where \(m\geq1\), and define
\[
v(x):=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(x).
\]
Then \(v\) is convex and its maximum is attained whenever \(v(x)<+\infty\). The active-index set
\[
I(x):=\{i:f_i(x)=v(x)\}
\]
is nonempty at every such \(x\). If all \(f_i\) are finite and continuous, then \(v\) is finite and continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximum of convex functions is convex and always has an active index at finite-valued points; continuity is inherited from finite continuous components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i\) is convex and \(I(x)\neq\varnothing\) whenever \(v(x)<+\infty\).

source_refs.locator: 5.3 Value Functions Associated with Convex Functions p. 268

source_witnesses.locator: 5.3 Value Functions Associated with Convex Functions p. 268

knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Parameter Max-Value Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact-parameter maximum theorem with continuity and upper hemicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(T\) be metric spaces, let \(T\) be nonempty and compact, and let \(\phi:X\times T\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous. Define
\[
v(x):=\max_{t\in T}\phi(x,t),\qquad M(x):=\operatorname*{argmax}_{t\in T}\phi(x,t).
\]
Then \(v\) is finite and continuous on \(X\). For every \(x\in X\), the set \(M(x)\) is nonempty and compact, and the correspondence \(M:X\rightrightarrows T\) is upper hemicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous objective maximized over a fixed compact parameter set has a continuous value and a nonempty compact, upper-hemicontinuous argmax correspondence.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(T\) are metric spaces, with \(T\) nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is continuous, and \(M(x)\) is nonempty, compact, and upper hemicontinuous in \(x\).

children.title: Nonattaining Maximizer Models
children.top_down_role: Max-value models whose optimizing parameters are not attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattaining Maximizer Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of maximizer existence on a noncompact parameter domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\{0\}\), let \(T=(0,1)\), and define \(\phi(0,t):=t\). The value is
\[
v(0):=\sup_{t\in T}\phi(0,t)=1,
\]
but
\[
\operatorname*{argmax}_{t\in T}\phi(0,t)=\varnothing.
\]
Thus continuity of the parameterized objective does not guarantee attainment when the parameter set is not compact. Every maximizing sequence \((t_k)\) satisfies \(t_k\to1\), whose limit lies outside \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the open interval, the continuous function t has supremum one but no maximizer, showing that compactness cannot simply be omitted from attainment results.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(0)=1\) while \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{t\in T}\phi(0,t)=\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct and fits the nonattainment leaf, but it has no citation or standard-field rationale.

children.title: Unstable Argmax Models
children.top_down_role: Models with abrupt or fragile changes in maximizing parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Unstable Argmax Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of a continuous maximizer selection at an active-set switch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=\mathbb{R}\), \(T=\{-1,1\}\), and \(\phi(x,t):=tx\). Then
\[
v(x)=\max_{t\in T}tx=|x|,
\]
and the argmax correspondence is
\[
M(x)=\{-1\}\ \text{if }x<0,\qquad M(0)=\{-1,1\},\qquad M(x)=\{1\}\ \text{if }x>0.
\]
Consequently, no single-valued selection \(s(x)\in M(x)\) can be continuous at \(0\), although \(T\) is finite and \(\phi\) and \(v\) are continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When two active branches exchange dominance, the value remains continuous but every maximizing selection jumps; argmax stability is stronger than value continuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no selection \(s:\mathbb{R}\to T\) with \(s(x)\in M(x)\) that is continuous at \(0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The active-branch example correctly rules out a continuous single-valued argmax selection at zero and fits the failure-boundary leaf, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Value Discontinuity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where parametric value behavior loses continuity.

knowledge_statements.title: Value Discontinuity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued discontinuity caused by a nonuniform infinite supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), define the continuous affine function \(f_n:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(f_n(x):=nx\), and let
\[
v(x):=\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}f_n(x).
\]
Then
\[
v(x)=x\ \text{for }x<0,\qquad v(0)=0,
\qquad v(x)=+\infty\ \text{for }x>0.
\]
Hence the supremum of continuous convex functions need not be finite or continuous. The failure occurs because the family is not locally bounded above near \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The supremum of the affine functions nx is finite to the left of zero but infinite to the right, so constituent continuity alone does not ensure value continuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(0)=0\), but \(v(x)=+\infty\) for every \(x>0\), so \(v\) is not continuous at \(0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied. Moreover, the formula for negative x is correct only if natural numbers begin at 1; if 0 is included, the supremum is 0 rather than x. The index domain must be made explicit.

children.title: Escaping-Parameter Regimes
children.top_down_role: Maximizing behavior associated with parameters escaping bounded regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Escaping-Parameter Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Argmax parameters escape to infinity as the base point approaches a limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X=T=\mathbb{R}\) and define \(\phi(x,t):=-(xt-1)^2\). For every \(x\neq0\),
\[
v(x):=\sup_{t\in T}\phi(x,t)=0,
\qquad M(x)=\{1/x\}.
\]
At \(x=0\), one has \(v(0)=-1\) and \(M(0)=\mathbb{R}\). Thus, for any sequence \(x_k\to0\) with \(x_k\neq0\), the unique maximizers \(t_k=1/x_k\) are unbounded. The argmax correspondence is not locally bounded at \(0\), and the value is discontinuous there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unique maximizers can diverge as the base point approaches a limit; without level compactness, argmax local boundedness and value continuity may both fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(x_k\to0\) and \(x_k\neq0\), then the maximizers \(t_k=1/x_k\) escape every bounded subset of \(T\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The calculations and escaping-maximizer conclusion are correct and fit the leaf, but the concrete counterexample has no supporting citation or standard-field rationale.

children.title: Polyhedral Piecewise Linear-Quadratic Convex Family

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Preservation of Convex Piecewise Linear-Quadratic Structure under Infimal Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers infimal convolution, linear-image value functions, and partial minimization, including the exceptional improper alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the input functions have the proper, convex, piecewise linear-quadratic properties specified in the corresponding clauses. Then f_1\mathbin{\#}f_2,\quad g(u)=\inf\{f(x)\mid Ax=u\},\quad\text{and}\quad p(u)=\inf_x f(x,u) are each proper, convex, and piecewise linear-quadratic unless the resulting function is improper with a polyhedral domain on which it is identically -\infty. In either case, the resulting function is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution, linear-image value functions, and partial minimization preserve convex piecewise linear-quadratic structure and lower semicontinuity. The stated exceptional result is an improper function equal to minus infinity throughout its polyhedral domain; it is still lower semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: f_1,f_2\text{ are proper, convex, and piecewise linear-quadratic in the infimal-convolution clause}
A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\text{ and }f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\text{ is proper, convex, and piecewise linear-quadratic in the linear-image clause}
f:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\text{ is proper, convex, and piecewise linear-quadratic in the partial-minimization clause}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each result is lsc and is either proper convex PLQ, or improper with a polyhedral domain on which it equals }-\infty.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Free Conjugate Formulas for Convex Piecewise Linear-Quadratic Functions
Polyhedral Convex Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real convex functions with polyhedral epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is polyhedral convex if its epigraph is a nonempty polyhedron. Equivalently, there exist a nonempty polyhedron \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and scalars \(b_1,\ldots,b_m\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\{\langle a_i,x\rangle+b_i\}\quad\text{for }x\in D,
\]
and \(f(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\notin D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function is polyhedral when its epigraph is a polyhedron, equivalently when it is a finite maximum of affine functions on a polyhedral domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is polyhedral convex exactly when \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a nonempty polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Piecewise Linear-Quadratic Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex extended-real functions represented quadratically on finitely many polyhedral pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex piecewise linear-quadratic if its domain is the union of finitely many polyhedra \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\) and, for each \(i\), there exist a symmetric matrix \(Q_i\), a vector \(q_i\), and a scalar \(r_i\) such that
\[
f(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Q_i x\rangle+\langle q_i,x\rangle+r_i
\quad\text{for }x\in P_i.
\]
The formulas must agree on overlaps; global convexity is part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex piecewise linear-quadratic function is proper, closed, and convex, with a quadratic formula on each member of a finite polyhedral cover of its domain.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On every \(P_i\), the function \(f\) agrees with a quadratic expression, consistently on overlaps.

notation.meaning: symmetric matrix of the ith quadratic piece

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral minimizers and PLQ value functions for convex PLQ programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural consequences of minimizing a convex PLQ function over a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be convex and PLQ, let $X\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a polyhedron, and define $v(c)=\min_{x\in X}\{f(x)+c^\top x\}$. Then: (i) if $\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)$ is nonempty, it is a polyhedron; (ii) $\operatorname{dom}v$ is a polyhedron; and (iii) $v$ is PLQ on $\operatorname{dom}v$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex PLQ objective over a polyhedron, every nonempty minimizer set is polyhedral. The finiteness domain of the linearly perturbed value function is polyhedral, and the value function is PLQ on that domain.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex and PLQ}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\text{ is a polyhedron};\quad\operatorname{dom}v\text{ is a polyhedron};\quad v\text{ is PLQ on }\operatorname{dom}v

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of convex piecewise linear-quadratic functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural equivalence involving subgradients, Moreau envelopes, and proximal mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For any $\lambda>0$, the following are equivalent: (a) $f$ is piecewise linear-quadratic; (b) $\partial f$ is piecewise polyhedral; (c) $e_\lambda f$ is piecewise linear-quadratic; and (d) $P_\lambda f$ is piecewise linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any positive parameter, a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function is piecewise linear-quadratic if and only if its subgradient mapping is piecewise polyhedral, its Moreau envelope is piecewise linear-quadratic, and its proximal mapping is piecewise linear.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is piecewise linear-quadratic}\iff\partial f\text{ is piecewise polyhedral}\iff e_\lambda f\text{ is piecewise linear-quadratic}\iff P_\lambda f\text{ is piecewise linear}.

children.title: Polyhedral Gauge Models
children.top_down_role: Positively homogeneous models generated by polyhedral gauge geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Gauge Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauges of absorbing polyhedra and their polar support representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a closed convex polyhedron with \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\). Its gauge is
\[
\gamma_C(x):=\inf\{\lambda\geq0:x\in\lambda C\}.
\]
For the polar polyhedron
\[
C^\circ:=\{y:\langle y,c\rangle\leq1\ \text{for all }c\in C\},
\]
one has \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\). Consequently, \(\gamma_C\) is finite, convex, positively homogeneous, and polyhedral. It need not satisfy \(\gamma_C(x)=\gamma_C(-x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of a closed convex polyhedron containing zero in its interior equals the support function of its polar; it is finite, convex, positively homogeneous, polyhedral, and generally asymmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C=\sigma_{C^\circ}\), and \(\gamma_C\) is a finite polyhedral convex gauge.

children.title: Polyhedral Norm Models
children.top_down_role: Norm objectives with polyhedral unit balls.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Norm Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Centrally symmetric polyhedral unit balls and finite absolute-linear maxima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a compact, convex, centrally symmetric polyhedron with \(0\in\operatorname{int}B\). Its gauge \(\|x\|_B:=\gamma_B(x)\) is a norm whose closed unit ball is \(B\). Conversely, every norm with a polyhedral unit ball arises this way. Equivalently, there exist vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) spanning \(\mathbb{R}^n\) such that
\[
\|x\|_B=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}|\langle a_i,x\rangle|.
\]
Thus polyhedral norms are convex piecewise-linear objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm is polyhedral exactly when its unit ball is a centrally symmetric polytope, equivalently when it is a finite maximum of absolute linear forms.
assumptions_latex: \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact, convex, centrally symmetric, and polyhedral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_B\) is a norm and admits a representation \(\gamma_B(x)=\max_i|\langle a_i,x\rangle|\) with spanning vectors \(a_i\).

children.title: Polar Polytope Geometry
children.top_down_role: Dual geometric structure associated with polyhedral gauges or norms.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is a full-dimensional compact convex polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^\circ\) is a polytope and \(\gamma_P(x)=\max_{y\in P^\circ}\langle y,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polar representation of a polyhedral gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the polar polytope by \(P^\circ:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^d:\langle y,x\rangle\leq 1\text{ for every }x\in P\}\) and the gauge by \(\gamma_P(x):=\inf\{t\geq0:x\in tP\}\). Then \(P^\circ\) is a compact full-dimensional polytope containing \(0\) in its interior, and the gauge is its support function: \[\gamma_P(x)=\sigma_{P^\circ}(x)=\max_{y\in P^\circ}\langle y,x\rangle=\max_{y\in\operatorname{vert}(P^\circ)}\langle y,x\rangle.\] Thus the facets of \(P\) determine vertices of \(P^\circ\), and conversely, under the inclusion-reversing polar face correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope containing the origin defines a gauge equal to the support function of its polar, hence to a finite maximum over polar vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Polar Polytope Geometry

children.title: Asymmetric Gauge Regimes
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral gauge models lacking norm symmetry.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is a compact convex set with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_P\) is a finite sublinear gauge but is not a norm because \(\gamma_P(x)\neq\gamma_P(-x)\) for some \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued asymmetric gauges generated by nonsymmetric convex bodies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(\gamma_P(x):=\inf\{t\geq0:x\in tP\}\). The function \(\gamma_P\) is finite, nonnegative, positively homogeneous for nonnegative scalars, and subadditive. Moreover, \(\gamma_P(x)=0\) holds only for \(x=0\). Symmetry is characterized exactly by the unit set: \[\gamma_P(x)=\gamma_P(-x)\text{ for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^d\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P=-P.\] Hence a nonsymmetric \(P\) yields an asymmetric gauge, and there is some \(x\) for which the forward and reverse costs \(\gamma_P(x)\) and \(\gamma_P(-x)\) differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsymmetric convex unit set produces a sublinear, positive-definite gauge whose cost can differ between opposite directions; symmetry holds exactly for centrally symmetric unit sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymmetric Gauge Regimes

children.title: Convex Loss Families
children.top_down_role: Nondifferentiable data-fit models grouped by residual, margin, robustness, and ordering structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Absolute loss and posterior medians
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bayes estimation of a real-valued state under absolute-deviation loss; the source's equal-half formula is a special case rather than the general median condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let H be real-valued and let \ell_1(h,a)=|h-a| for a\in\mathbb R. If \mathbb E[|H|\mid x]<\infty, then the minimizers of the posterior risk \mathbb E[|H-a|\mid x] are exactly the posterior medians: \operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathbb R}\mathbb E[|H-a|\mid x]=\{a:\Pr(H\le a\mid x)\ge \tfrac12,\ \Pr(H\ge a\mid x)\ge \tfrac12\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolute-deviation loss is the absolute difference between a real state and action. When the posterior first moment is finite, its Bayes-optimal actions are exactly the posterior medians. Equal probabilities on the two sides hold only under additional distributional conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{a\in\mathbb R}\mathbb E[|H-a|\mid x]=\left\{a:\Pr(H\le a\mid x)\ge\tfrac12,\ \Pr(H\ge a\mid x)\ge\tfrac12\right\}

children.title: Absolute-Deviation Losses
children.top_down_role: Symmetric deviation losses with a central kink.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell(r)=|r|=\max\{r,-r\}\), with \(\partial\ell(0)=[-1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar absolute-deviation loss and its unique kink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The absolute-deviation loss is the convex piecewise-affine function \[\ell(r):=|r|=\max\{r,-r\}=\begin{cases}-r,&r<0,\\ r,&r\geq0.\end{cases}\] Its convex subdifferential is \[\partial\ell(r)=\begin{cases}\{-1\},&r<0,\\ [-1,1],&r=0,\\ \{1\},&r>0.\end{cases}\] Consequently, the loss grows linearly in the magnitude of the residual and is nondifferentiable only at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolute-deviation loss is the residual magnitude. It is convex and piecewise affine, with slopes minus one and one and subdifferential interval [-1,1] at zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Absolute-Deviation Losses

children.title: Quantile Check Losses
children.top_down_role: Asymmetric piecewise-linear losses indexed by a quantile level.

assumptions_latex: \(r\in\mathbb{R}\) is a residual defined as observation minus prediction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_\tau(r)=\max\{\tau r,-(1-\tau)r\}\), with \(\partial\rho_\tau(0)=[\tau-1,\tau]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard observation-minus-prediction convention for quantile loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a quantile level \(\tau\in(0,1)\), the check loss is \[\rho_\tau(r):=r\bigl(\tau-\mathbf{1}_{\{r<0\}}\bigr)=\begin{cases}(\tau-1)r,&r<0,\\ \tau r,&r\geq0,\end{cases}=\max\{\tau r,-(1-\tau)r\}.\] It is convex, positively homogeneous, and piecewise affine. Its convex subdifferential is \(\partial\rho_\tau(r)=\{\tau-1\}\) for \(r<0\), \(\partial\rho_\tau(0)=[\tau-1,\tau]\), and \(\partial\rho_\tau(r)=\{\tau\}\) for \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quantile check loss weights positive residuals by tau and negative residual magnitudes by one minus tau; its kink subdifferential spans from tau minus one to tau.
knowledge_statements.title: Quantile Check Losses

children.title: Median Regression Interface
children.top_down_role: Regression models centered on median-oriented loss structure.

assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is an integrable real-valued random variable.
\(X\) is a covariate, and conditional statements are interpreted almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\in\arg\min_{a\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}[|Y-a|\mid X]\) almost surely exactly when \(M\) is a conditional median of \(Y\) given \(X\).

notation.meaning: Candidate conditional location measurable with respect to the covariate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Population characterization underlying least-absolute-deviation regression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A real-valued \(\sigma(X)\)-measurable random variable \(M\) satisfies \[M\in\arg\min_{a\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{E}[|Y-a|\mid X]\] almost surely if and only if it is a conditional median, meaning \[\mathbb{P}(Y\leq M\mid X)\geq\tfrac12\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbb{P}(Y\geq M\mid X)\geq\tfrac12\] almost surely. Consequently, given observations \((x_i,y_i)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\) and a parametric predictor \(m_\beta\), minimizing \(\sum_{i=1}^n|y_i-m_\beta(x_i)|\) is the empirical least-absolute-deviation interface to conditional median regression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A covariate-measurable conditional location minimizes conditional expected absolute deviation exactly when it is a conditional median. Restricting that location to a parametric predictor yields least-absolute-deviation median regression.
knowledge_statements.title: Median Regression Interface

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Laplace Linear Regression as an Absolute-Deviation Linear Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-scale Laplace linear regression and the epigraph linear-program representation of its maximum-likelihood estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b>0\), let \((\mathbf x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^N\subseteq\mathbb R^D\times\mathbb R\), and suppose the observations are conditionally independent with \[p(y_i\mid\mathbf x_i,\mathbf w,b)=\operatorname{Laplace}(y_i\mid\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x_i,b)\propto\exp\!\left(-\frac{|y_i-\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x_i|}{b}\right).\] Then maximum-likelihood estimation of \(\mathbf w\) is equivalent to \[\min_{\mathbf w}\sum_{i=1}^N|y_i-\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x_i|.\] An equivalent linear program is \[\min_{\mathbf w,\mathbf e}\sum_{i=1}^Ne_i\quad\text{s.t.}\quad e_i\geq\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x_i-y_i,\qquad e_i\geq-(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x_i-y_i),\quad i=1,\ldots,N.\] Every optimal solution satisfies \(e_i=|y_i-\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x_i|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For conditionally independent observations with a fixed positive Laplace scale, maximum-likelihood linear regression minimizes the sum of absolute residuals. Introducing one epigraph variable per residual gives an equivalent linear program with two inequalities per observation, which are tight in the epigraph variable at an optimum.
assumptions_latex: y_1,\ldots,y_N\text{ are conditionally independent given }(\mathbf x_1,\ldots,\mathbf x_N,\mathbf w,b)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{\mathbf w}\prod_{i=1}^Np(y_i\mid\mathbf x_i,\mathbf w,b)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathbf w,\mathbf e}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^Ne_i:\ e_i\geq\pm(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x_i-y_i)\ \forall i\right\}

children.title: Tail-Asymmetry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Quantile-loss behavior near strongly asymmetric tail levels.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive and negative residual magnitudes receive respective weights \(\tau\) and \(1-\tau\), equal only when \(\tau=\tfrac12\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymmetry induced by the quantile level under a fixed residual convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(r=y-q\), the check loss satisfies \[\rho_\tau(r)=\tau r\quad\text{when }r\geq0,\qquad \rho_\tau(r)=(1-\tau)|r|\quad\text{when }r<0.\] Thus \(\tau>\tfrac12\) penalizes underprediction more heavily than equal-magnitude overprediction, whereas \(\tau<\tfrac12\) reverses this preference. The loss is symmetric exactly at \(\tau=\tfrac12\), where \(\rho_{1/2}(r)=\tfrac12|r|\). As \(\tau\) approaches \(1\) or \(0\), one residual direction receives vanishing slope, producing increasingly one-sided tail sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quantile level determines unequal slopes on the two residual tails. Levels above one half emphasize underprediction; levels below one half emphasize overprediction.
knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Asymmetry Regimes

children.title: Hinge Losses
children.top_down_role: Piecewise-linear losses generated by thresholded residuals.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\mathrm{hinge}}(y,s)=\max\{0,1-ys\}\), with a nondifferentiable point at \(ys=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-margin binary hinge loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The binary hinge loss is \[\ell_{\mathrm{hinge}}(y,s):=(1-ys)_+=\max\{0,1-ys\}.\] Writing \(m=ys\), its margin subdifferential is \[\partial_m(1-m)_+=\begin{cases}\{-1\},&m<1,\\ [-1,0],&m=1,\\ \{0\},&m>1.\end{cases}\] Hence the loss is convex and piecewise affine in the margin, penalizes every observation with margin below one, vanishes for margins at least one, and is nondifferentiable at the unit-margin boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary hinge loss is the positive part of one minus the signed margin. It vanishes beyond unit margin and has a kink at the unit-margin boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Hinge Losses

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hinge loss and zero-one-loss upper bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-label hinge loss with a positive margin parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\gamma>0\), \(p\in\mathbb R\), and \(y\in\{-1,1\}\), the hinge loss is \(\ell_\gamma(p,y)=(\gamma-py)_+\). It is convex as a function of \(p\), and its normalized value upper-bounds the zero-one loss: \(\ell_{01}(p,y)\leq \ell_\gamma(p,y)/\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hinge loss is the positive part of gamma minus the signed prediction. It is convex in the prediction, and its value divided by gamma upper-bounds binary zero-one loss.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell_\gamma(p,y)=(\gamma-py)_+,\qquad p\mapsto\ell_\gamma(p,y)\text{ is convex},\qquad \ell_{01}(p,y)\leq\frac{\ell_\gamma(p,y)}{\gamma}.

children.title: Margin-Based Losses
children.top_down_role: Classification losses organized through signed margins.

assumptions_latex: \(\phi:\mathbb{R}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, and nonincreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell(y,s)=\phi(ys)\) is a convex loss in \(s\) determined solely by the signed margin.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary convex losses depending only on signed margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary margin-based loss has the form \[\ell(y,s):=\phi(ys),\] where \(m=ys\) is the signed margin and \(\phi\) is a nonincreasing loss profile. If \(\phi\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, then \(s\mapsto\ell(y,s)\) is convex for each fixed \(y\). At any finite margin \(m\), its score subdifferential obeys \[\partial_s\ell(y,s)=y\,\partial\phi(m).\] Piecewise-affine profiles, including \(\phi(m)=(1-m)_+\), generate nonsmooth convex objectives through changes in active affine pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary margin loss applies a nonincreasing convex profile to the signed margin. Piecewise-affine profiles produce convex losses with kinks where the active piece changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Margin-Based Losses

children.title: Multiclass Margin Variants
children.top_down_role: Margin losses adapted to multiple competing classes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_{\mathrm{CS}}(y,s)=\max\{0,\max_{j\neq y}(1+s_j-s_y)\}\) is convex and piecewise affine in \(s\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crammer-Singer unit-margin multiclass hinge variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For class scores \(s=(s_1,\ldots,s_K)\) and observed class \(y\), the Crammer-Singer multiclass hinge loss is \[\ell_{\mathrm{CS}}(y,s):=\max\left\{0,\max_{j\neq y}\{1+s_j-s_y\}\right\}.\] It is the maximum of finitely many affine functions of \(s\), hence is convex and piecewise affine. It vanishes exactly when \(s_y\geq 1+s_j\) for every \(j\neq y\). Nondifferentiability occurs when several competing classes attain the maximum or when the maximal margin violation equals zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Crammer-Singer loss takes the largest positive unit-margin violation among competing classes. It is convex, piecewise affine, and nonsmooth at ties or activation boundaries.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiclass Margin Variants

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiclass margin and empirical margin loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Score-based mono-label multiclass classification, with ties counted as errors for the stated margin characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $h:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R$, define $\rho_h(x,y)=h(x,y)-\max_{y'\ne y}h(x,y')$. Under the convention that a tie with a competing class counts as an error, $(x,y)$ is misclassified if and only if $\rho_h(x,y)\le0$. For $\rho>0$ and a sample $((x_i,y_i))_{i=1}^m$, define $\widehat R_\rho(h)=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\Phi_\rho(\rho_h(x_i,y_i))$. Then $\widehat R_\rho(h)\le\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{\rho_h(x_i,y_i)\le\rho\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The multiclass margin is the true-label score minus the largest competing-label score. When ties count as errors, nonpositive margin is equivalent to misclassification. The empirical margin loss is bounded above by the fraction of sample points whose margin is at most rho.
assumptions_latex: \text{ties with competing classes are counted as misclassifications}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_h(x,y)\le0\iff (x,y)\text{ is misclassified},\qquad \widehat R_\rho(h)\le\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{\rho_h(x_i,y_i)\le\rho\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized Multiclass Hinge Loss and Its Basic Properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, prediction-loss upper bound, margin equality regime, convexity, and Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \Delta:\mathcal Y\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R_+ with \Delta(y,y)=0, and choose h_{\mathbf w}(\mathbf x)\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{y'\in\mathcal Y}\langle\mathbf w,\Psi(\mathbf x,y')\rangle. Define
\[
\ell(\mathbf w;(\mathbf x,y))=\max_{y'\in\mathcal Y}\left\{\Delta(y',y)+\left\langle\mathbf w,\Psi(\mathbf x,y')-\Psi(\mathbf x,y)\right\rangle\right\}.
\]
Then \ell(\mathbf w;(\mathbf x,y))\geq\Delta(h_{\mathbf w}(\mathbf x),y). The function \ell(\cdot;(\mathbf x,y)) is convex and, when \rho=\max_{y'\in\mathcal Y}\|\Psi(\mathbf x,y')-\Psi(\mathbf x,y)\|_2<\infty, is \rho-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm. Equality with the prediction loss holds if \langle\mathbf w,\Psi(\mathbf x,y)\rangle\geq\langle\mathbf w,\Psi(\mathbf x,y')\rangle+\Delta(y',y) for every y'\neq y.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized multiclass hinge loss maximizes the misclassification cost plus a competing label's score advantage. It convexly upper-bounds the actual prediction loss, is Lipschitz with a feature-difference bound, and equals the prediction loss in the stated cost-scaled margin regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell(\mathbf w;(\mathbf x,y))\geq\Delta(h_{\mathbf w}(\mathbf x),y),\qquad \ell(\cdot;(\mathbf x,y))\text{ is convex and }\rho\text{-Lipschitz}.

children.title: Zero-Margin Kink Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nonsmooth regimes occurring at active margin thresholds.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_0(m)=(-m)_+\) has \(\partial h_0(0)=[-1,0]\), so the active-set transition occurs at zero margin.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-threshold hinge, distinguished from the usual unit-margin hinge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The zero-threshold hinge profile is \[h_0(m):=(-m)_+=\max\{0,-m\}.\] Its convex subdifferential is \[\partial h_0(m)=\begin{cases}\{-1\},&m<0,\\ [-1,0],&m=0,\\ \{0\},&m>0.\end{cases}\] Thus negative margins are penalized linearly, positive margins incur no loss, and zero margin is the kink at which the active affine piece changes. More generally, \((a-m)_+\) has its kink at \(m=a\); the zero-margin regime is precisely the choice \(a=0\), not the standard unit-margin choice \(a=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With threshold zero, hinge loss penalizes negative margins and vanishes for positive margins. Its kink and set-valued subgradient occur exactly at zero margin.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Margin Kink Regimes

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Huber loss is quadratic for \(|r|\leq\delta\), affine in \(|r|\) outside, and has derivative clipped to \([-\delta,\delta]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Huber loss as a canonical robust piecewise linear-quadratic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For threshold \(\delta>0\), the Huber loss is \[H_\delta(r):=\begin{cases}\tfrac12r^2,&|r|\leq\delta,\\ \delta|r|-\tfrac12\delta^2,&|r|>\delta.\end{cases}\] It is finite, convex, continuously differentiable, and piecewise linear-quadratic, with derivative \[H_\delta'(r)=\begin{cases}-\delta,&r<-\delta,\\ r,&|r|\leq\delta,\\ \delta,&r>\delta.\end{cases}\] The bounded derivative limits the marginal influence of large residuals, while the quadratic central region retains local squared-error behavior. The piece boundaries occur at \(r=\pm\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Huber loss is quadratic near zero and linear in large residual magnitude. Its clipped derivative bounds the influence of outliers while preserving squared-error behavior centrally.
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Piecewise Losses

children.title: Ordered-Statistic Losses
children.top_down_role: Losses organized by sorted component values.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_w(z)=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i z_{[i]}=\max_{\pi\in S_n}\sum_{i=1}^n w_i z_{\pi(i)}\), so \(L_w\) is convex and piecewise affine.

notation.meaning: Components of z sorted in nonincreasing order

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex ordered weighted sum under nonincreasing nonnegative weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_{[1]}\geq\cdots\geq z_{[n]}\) denote the components of \(z\) arranged in nonincreasing order. For weights \(w_1\geq\cdots\geq w_n\geq0\), define \[L_w(z):=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i z_{[i]}.\] The rearrangement representation is \[L_w(z)=\max_{\pi\in S_n}\sum_{i=1}^n w_i z_{\pi(i)}.\] Therefore \(L_w\) is a finite maximum of affine functions and is convex and piecewise affine. At vectors with tied components, multiple maximizing permutations may coexist, producing a set-valued subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonincreasing weighted sum of descending order statistics equals a maximum over permutations. This makes the loss convex, piecewise affine, and potentially nonsmooth at ties.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordered-Statistic Losses

children.title: Top-k Losses
children.top_down_role: Losses retaining the largest selected component values.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_k(z)=\max_{|I|=k}\sum_{i\in I}z_i=\max\{u^\top z:0\le u\le 1,\ \mathbf{1}^\top u=k\}\), so \(T_k\) is convex and piecewise linear.

notation.meaning: Components of z arranged in nonincreasing order.
Sum of the k largest component losses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the unnormalized sum of the \(k\) largest finite-dimensional losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z_{[1]}\ge\cdots\ge z_{[m]}\) denote the decreasing rearrangement of \(z\). The unnormalized top-k loss is
\[
T_k(z):=\sum_{j=1}^k z_{[j]}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
T_k(z)=\max_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\},\ |I|=k}\sum_{i\in I}z_i
=\max_{u\in[0,1]^m,\ \mathbf{1}^\top u=k}u^\top z.
\]
Thus \(T_k\) is the support function of \(\{u\in[0,1]^m:\mathbf{1}^\top u=k\}\), hence is finite, convex, permutation invariant, and piecewise linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The top-k loss sums the k largest component losses and equals a maximum over either k-element subsets or capped simplex weights.
knowledge_statements.title: Top-k Losses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and finite-dimensional support-function representation are mathematically precise, and the definition content kind fits the leaf, but no inspectable citation supports the selected top-k convention and stated properties.

children.title: Aggregate Tail Losses
children.top_down_role: Aggregations emphasizing upper or lower ordered tails.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_a(z)=\sum_{j=1}^m a_jz_{[j]}=\sum_{k=1}^m(a_k-a_{k+1})T_k(z)\) is convex, where \(a_{m+1}=0\).

notation.meaning: Sum of the k largest components.
Ordered tail-aggregation loss with weights a.
Decreasing rearrangement of the component losses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers finite ordered weighted aggregation emphasizing the upper loss tail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For decreasing nonnegative weights \(a_1\ge\cdots\ge a_m\ge0\), define
\[
A_a(z):=\sum_{j=1}^m a_jz_{[j]}.
\]
With \(a_{m+1}:=0\) and \(T_k(z):=\sum_{j=1}^kz_{[j]}\), summation by parts gives
\[
A_a(z)=\sum_{k=1}^m(a_k-a_{k+1})T_k(z).
\]
Every coefficient in this representation is nonnegative. Consequently, \(A_a\) is a nonnegative combination of top-k losses and is therefore convex, finite, permutation invariant, and piecewise linear on \(\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing nonnegative weighted sum of ordered losses is a nonnegative combination of top-k losses and therefore forms a convex upper-tail aggregate.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Tail Losses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ordered-weight representation and convexity conclusion are standard and internally consistent, and representation is the correct content kind, but the record supplies no citation for the ordered tail-aggregation formula.

children.title: Tie-Sensitive Ordering Regimes
children.top_down_role: Ordering regimes where equal component values create active-set ambiguity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial F(z)=\operatorname{conv}\{P^\top a:Pz=(z_{[1]},\ldots,z_{[m]})\}\); ties generally make this set non-singleton.

notation.meaning: Set of permutation matrices that sort z in nonincreasing order.
Convex subdifferential of F at z.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes convex subgradients at tied order statistics in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{P}(z)\) be the permutation matrices \(P\) satisfying \(Pz=(z_{[1]},\ldots,z_{[m]})\). Since
\[
F(z)=\max_{P\in\mathcal{P}_m}a^\top Pz,
\]
the active-affine subgradient rule yields
\[
\partial F(z)=\operatorname{conv}\{P^\top a:P\in\mathcal{P}(z)\}.
\]
If the components of \(z\) are distinct, the sorting permutation is unique, apart from equal weights. If a tie block crosses positions carrying unequal weights, multiple permutations are active and \(F\) is nondifferentiable there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a tie, every ordering consistent with the tied values is active; the subdifferential is the convex hull of their assigned weight vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Sensitive Ordering Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The active-permutation subdifferential formula is plausible and the property kind fits, but it requires an authoritative source. The phrase 'unique, apart from equal weights' should also be clarified: distinct components give a unique sorting permutation, while equal weights can make gradients coincide.

children.top_down_role: Constraint, domain, distance, and violation structures represented inside an objective.

children.title: Indicator-Function Constrained Model
children.top_down_role: The extended-valued bridge between constrained and unconstrained model architectures.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and \(\inf_x(f(x)+\delta_C(x))=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Extended-real indicator of C, equal to zero on C and positive infinity outside C.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real representation of a closed convex feasibility constraint.

source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the extended-real indicator of \(C\) by
\[
\delta_C(x):=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(\delta_C:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For every extended-real objective \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\),
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+\delta_C(x)\bigr)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x),
\]
with equality also holding for the corresponding infimal values under the convention \(+\infty+a=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex constraint is encoded by adding its zero-or-infinity indicator; unconstrained minimization of the extended objective is equivalent to minimization over the set.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Set Indicator Models

source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex-Set Indicator Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real modeling for closed feasibility sets without assuming convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed set \(C\subseteq X\), define
\[
\delta_C(x):=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}
\]
Then \(\delta_C:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, and it is convex if and only if \(C\) is convex. For every \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\),
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+\delta_C(x)\bigr)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x),
\]
and the corresponding infimal values are equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extended-real indicator represents any nonempty closed constraint exactly, including a nonconvex constraint; it is convex precisely when the constraint set is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, is convex exactly when \(C\) is convex, and adding it to \(f\) represents minimization over \(C\).

children.title: Product-Set Indicator Models
children.top_down_role: Indicator objectives built from Cartesian product constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(X_i\) are finite-dimensional spaces and \(C_i\subseteq X_i\) are nonempty for \(i=1,\ldots,p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C(x_1,\ldots,x_p)=\sum_{i=1}^p\delta_{C_i}(x_i)\).

notation.meaning: Cartesian product of the factor constraint sets.
Extended-real indicator of a set D.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian-product constraints and their additive indicator representation.

source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_p)\) in \(X:=X_1\times\cdots\times X_p\), membership in \(C:=C_1\times\cdots\times C_p\) holds exactly when \(x_i\in C_i\) for every \(i\). Therefore, using extended-real addition,
\[
\delta_C(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p\delta_{C_i}(x_i).
\]
If every \(C_i\) is closed, then \(C\) and \(\delta_C\) are closed. If every \(C_i\) is convex, then \(C\) and \(\delta_C\) are convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of a Cartesian product equals the sum of the factor indicators, so product feasibility is represented coordinate by coordinate.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Set Indicator Models

children.title: Intersection-Set Indicator Models
children.top_down_role: Indicator objectives representing simultaneous set membership.

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_p\) are subsets of a common finite-dimensional space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_C(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p\delta_{C_i}(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: Extended-real indicator of a set D.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite intersections represented by indicators evaluated at one shared decision variable.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Sequential Normal Compactness of Set Intersections and Inverse Images p. 341
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the convention for extended-real addition, the indicator of a finite intersection satisfies
\[
\delta_{\cap_{i=1}^pC_i}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p\delta_{C_i}(x),\qquad x\in X.
\]
Indeed, both sides equal \(0\) exactly when \(x\) belongs to every \(C_i\), and equal \(+\infty\) otherwise. Hence adding the individual indicators to an objective imposes all constraints simultaneously, even when the intersection is empty or some sets are nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of an intersection equals the sum of indicators evaluated at the same point, thereby coupling all constraints through one decision variable.

children.title: Product-Factor Separability
children.top_down_role: Decomposable indicator structure across Cartesian factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Factor Separability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise projection and proximal separability for Cartesian-product constraints in finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X_i\) be finite-dimensional real Hilbert spaces, equip \(X:=X_1\times\cdots\times X_p\) with
\[
\|x\|^2:=\sum_{i=1}^p\|x_i\|_i^2,
\]
and let \(C:=C_1\times\cdots\times C_p\), where every \(C_i\subseteq X_i\) is nonempty and closed. Then
\[
d_C(x)^2=\sum_{i=1}^p d_{C_i}(x_i)^2
\]
and the possibly set-valued metric projection factors as
\[
P_C(x)=P_{C_1}(x_1)\times\cdots\times P_{C_p}(x_p).
\]
For every \(\lambda>0\),
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\delta_C}(x)=P_C(x).
\]
If every \(C_i\) is convex, each factor projection and hence \(P_C\) are single-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the Hilbert product norm, distance, metric projection, and the indicator proximal map separate across Cartesian-product factors; convex factors give unique projections.
assumptions_latex: \(X_i\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space for \(i=1,\ldots,p\).
\(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_p\), where every \(C_i\subseteq X_i\) is nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C(x)=P_{C_1}(x_1)\times\cdots\times P_{C_p}(x_p)\) and \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda\delta_C}(x)=P_C(x)\) for every \(\lambda>0\).

notation.meaning: Possibly set-valued metric projection onto D.

children.top_down_role: Coupling created by multiple sets constraining shared variables.

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_p\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of a finite-dimensional space.

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic normal cone to D at x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex normal-cone coupling under the relative-interior qualification.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Sequential Normal Compactness of Set Intersections and Inverse Images p. 341
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C:=\bigcap_{i=1}^pC_i\). If the relative-interior qualification
\[
\bigcap_{i=1}^p\operatorname{ri}C_i\ne\varnothing
\]
holds, then for every \(x\in C\),
\[
N_C(x)=\sum_{i=1}^pN_{C_i}(x).
\]
Equivalently, every normal to the coupled intersection can be decomposed as a sum of normals contributed by the individual constraints. Without an appropriate qualification, only the inclusion \(\sum_iN_{C_i}(x)\subseteq N_C(x)\) is automatic in the convex setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a relative-interior qualification, the normal cone to an intersection is exactly the sum of the individual normal cones.

children.title: Distance Penalty Models
children.top_down_role: Penalty objectives based on distance to a target set.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space and \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_\rho(x)=f(x)+\rho d_C(x)\), where \(d_C(x)=0\) exactly on \(C\) and \(d_C\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear distance penalty for a nonempty closed feasibility set.

source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The distance to \(C\) is
\[
d_C(x):=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|,
\]
and the linear distance-penalty model is
\[
F_\rho(x):=f(x)+\rho d_C(x).
\]
Because \(C\) is closed, \(d_C(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\in C\). Moreover, \(d_C\) is finite, nonnegative, and \(1\)-Lipschitz. If \(C\) is convex, then \(d_C\) is convex; consequently \(F_\rho\) is convex whenever \(f\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distance penalty adds a positive multiple of distance to the feasible set; the penalty vanishes exactly at feasible points and is always Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance Penalty Models

source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Feasibility Residual Penalties
children.top_down_role: Penalty objectives based on residual measures of constraint satisfaction.

assumptions_latex: \(g_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(h_j:X\to\mathbb{R}\) define inequality and equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(x)=0\iff x\in C\), and \(f(x)+\rho R(x)\) penalizes the largest displayed violation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum residual for finitely many inequalities and equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the maximum feasibility residual by
\[
R(x):=\max\bigl\{[g_1(x)]_+,\ldots,[g_r(x)]_+,|h_1(x)|,\ldots,|h_s(x)|\bigr\},
\]
where \([t]_+:=\max\{t,0\}\). Then \(R(x)\ge0\) and
\[
R(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in C.
\]
Thus \(f(x)+\rho R(x)\) is an unconstrained residual-penalty representation of the constrained model. If every \(g_i\) is convex and every \(h_j\) is affine, then \(R\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum of positive inequality violations and absolute equality residuals is zero exactly at feasible points and supplies a nonsmooth feasibility penalty.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Residual Penalties

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximum-residual construction is standard and representation fits the leaf, but no source is supplied. A sourced version should also quantify the finite constraint counts r and s and specify the index domains of the two constraint families.

children.title: Exact-Penalty Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where penalized models preserve constrained solutions.

assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in C\) locally minimizes \(f\) over a closed set \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\rho>L\kappa\), \(\bar x\) locally minimizes \(f+\rho R\); every feasible local minimizer of \(f+\rho R\) locally minimizes \(f\) over \(C\).

notation.meaning: Feasibility residual with zero set C.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local exactness derived from Lipschitz continuity and a residual error bound.

source_refs.locator: 5.2.3 Refined Lower Subdifferential Conditions for MPECs via Exact Penalization p. 61
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(\bar x\in C\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\), \(f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), and the local error bound
\[
d_C(x)\le\kappa R(x)
\]
holds near \(\bar x\), where \(R\ge0\) and \(R^{-1}(0)=C\). Then, for every \(\rho>L\kappa\), \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(f+\rho R\). Conversely, any feasible local minimizer of \(f+\rho R\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lipschitz objective and local residual error bound make the residual penalty locally exact once the penalty parameter exceeds the Lipschitz-error-bound threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Penalty Regimes

children.title: Inconsistent-Feasibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Penalty behavior when the underlying constraints have no common feasible point.

knowledge_statements.title: Inconsistent-Feasibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance penalties when the underlying closed convex constraints have no common feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) be nonempty closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(w_i>0\), and define \(P(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i d(x,C_i)\). Then \(P\) is finite and convex, and \(P(x)=0\) holds exactly when \(x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\). Consequently, if \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i=\varnothing\), no point has zero penalty, although the infimum of \(P\) need not be positive or attained. Minimizing \(P\) is therefore a best-compromise problem rather than an exact feasibility reformulation. For example, with \(C_1=(-\infty,0]\) and \(C_2=[1,\infty)\), one has \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}} d(x,C_1)+d(x,C_2)=1\), attained by every \(x\in[0,1]\), although no feasible point exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With inconsistent constraints, a sum of distances has no zero-penalty point and serves as a best-compromise objective; its infimum is not necessarily positive or attained. Two separated half-lines give an explicit case with positive attained minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \(P(x)=0\); minimizers, when present, are compromise points rather than feasible points.

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance from x to C

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary distance-function properties and an explicit one-dimensional example

children.title: Scalar Violation Penalties
children.top_down_role: Penalty models driven by scalar measures of constraint violation.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Violation Penalties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar penalties for one inequality or equality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scalar inequality constraint \(g(x)\leq 0\), its positive-part violation is \(v_g(x)=[g(x)]_+=\max\{g(x),0\}\), and a weighted scalar penalty is \(P_g(x)=\rho\,\phi(v_g(x))\), where \(\rho>0\), \(\phi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]\), \(\phi(0)=0\), and \(\phi(t)>0\) for \(t>0\). For an equality constraint \(h(x)=0\), one may analogously set \(v_h(x)=|h(x)|\) and \(P_h(x)=\rho\,\phi(v_h(x))\). In each case the penalty vanishes exactly when the represented scalar constraint is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar constraint is penalized by applying a nonnegative penalty function to its positive-part or absolute violation, with zero penalty exactly at satisfaction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_g(x)=0\iff g(x)\leq0\), and \(P_h(x)=0\iff h(x)=0\).

children.title: Composite Penalty Architectures
children.top_down_role: Penalty models formed by composing violation maps with outer penalties.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Penalty Architectures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer penalty functions composed with vector-valued violation maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}_+^m\) be a violation map satisfying \(v(x)=0\) exactly on a feasible set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). A composite penalty architecture has the form \(P(x)=\rho\,\Phi(v(x))\), where \(\rho>0\) and \(\Phi:\mathbb{R}_+^m\to[0,\infty]\) satisfies \(\Phi(0)=0\) and \(\Phi(z)>0\) for every \(z\neq0\). Thus \(P(x)=0\) exactly on \(S\). If every component \(v_i\) is convex and \(\Phi\) is convex and coordinatewise nondecreasing on \(\mathbb{R}_+^m\), then \(P\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector of constraint violations is passed through an outer aggregator. Positivity gives exact zero detection, while convexity of the components and convex coordinatewise monotonicity of the outer function preserve convexity.
assumptions_latex: For the convexity conclusion, every \(v_i\) is convex and \(\Phi\) is convex and coordinatewise nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{-1}(0)=S\); under the stated component-convexity and outer convex-monotonicity assumptions, \(P\) is convex.

notation.meaning: the i-th component of the violation map
feasible set detected by zero violation

children.title: Multiple-Constraint Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Structures for combining penalties from several constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Constraint Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard sum and maximum aggregations of finitely many constraint violations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given nonnegative violations \(v_i(x)\geq0\) and weights \(w_i>0\), two standard aggregate penalties are \(P_1(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i v_i(x)\) and \(P_\infty(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m} w_i v_i(x)\). Both satisfy \(P_1(x)=0\iff P_\infty(x)=0\iff v_i(x)=0\) for every \(i\). If all \(v_i\) are convex, then both aggregates are convex. Moreover, with \(w_{\min}=\min_i w_i\) and \(w_{\max}=\max_i w_i\), \(w_{\min}\max_i v_i(x)\leq P_1(x)\leq m w_{\max}\max_i v_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive weighted sums and maxima detect simultaneous satisfaction of all constraints, preserve convexity, and are quantitatively equivalent for finitely many violations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_1^{-1}(0)=P_\infty^{-1}(0)=\bigcap_i v_i^{-1}(0)\), with the displayed finite-dimensional comparison bounds.

children.title: Degenerate Penalty Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where penalty structure fails to distinguish relevant violations.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Penalty Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of constraint detection caused by zero weights or nonseparating outer penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_i:X\to[0,\infty)\) and let the feasible set be \(S=\{x\in X:v_i(x)=0\text{ for every }i\}\). For \(P(x)=\Phi(w_1v_1(x),\ldots,w_mv_m(x))\), zero detection can fail if a weight vanishes or if \(\Phi\) has a nonzero zero. If \(w_j=0\), the penalty is insensitive to \(v_j\); for example, with \(X=\mathbb{R}\), \(m=1\), \(v_1(x)=|x|\), \(w_1=0\), and \(\Phi(t)=t\), one has \(P(x)=0\) for every \(x\), although \(S=\{0\}\). Likewise, if \(z\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\setminus\{0\}\) satisfies \(\Phi(z)=0\), then any \(x\notin S\) whose weighted violation vector equals \(z\) is unpenalized. Conversely, if every \(w_i>0\) and \(\Phi^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\), then \(P(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero weight can hide a violated constraint, and an outer penalty with a nonzero zero can leave a realizable nonzero violation vector unpenalized. Positive weights and a unique outer zero guarantee exact zero detection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Zero weights or realizable nonzero elements of \(\Phi^{-1}(0)\) can cause false zero penalties; if every \(w_i>0\) and \(\Phi^{-1}(0)=\{0\}\), then \(P^{-1}(0)=S\).

notation.meaning: joint feasible set detected by the violations

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct consequences of the composite penalty formula with explicit counterexamples

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate-Generated Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objectives obtained as Fenchel conjugates of extended-real convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. Its Fenchel conjugate is the objective \(f^*:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) defined by \(f^*(y)=\sup_{x\in X}\{\langle y,x\rangle-f(x)\}\). Because it is a pointwise supremum of affine continuous functions of \(y\), \(f^*\) is convex and lower semicontinuous, even when \(f\) is not convex. If \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, then \(f^{**}=f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conjugate-generated objective is the supremum of affine minorant gaps; it is always closed convex, and conjugating twice recovers any proper closed convex function.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
For biconjugacy, \(f\) is also lower semicontinuous and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*\) is convex and lower semicontinuous; under the additional closed-convex assumptions, \(f^{**}=f\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard finite-dimensional Fenchel conjugacy definition and biconjugacy statement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conjugate formula, convexity, lower semicontinuity, and finite-dimensional biconjugacy statement are standard and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source locator supports the nontrivial claims. The phrase “affine minorant gaps” in the plain statement also needs source or terminology correction.

knowledge_statements.title: Infimal-Convolution Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real objectives formed by optimally decomposing an argument between two component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For functions \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) on a finite-dimensional vector space, their infimal convolution is \((f\mathbin{\square}g)(x)=\inf_{u\in X}\{f(u)+g(x-u)\}\). It is proper whenever this infimum is finite somewhere and never equals \(-\infty\). If \(f\) and \(g\) are convex, then \(f\mathbin{\square}g\) is convex. When the infimum is attained at \(u_x\), the value decomposes as \((f\mathbin{\square}g)(x)=f(u_x)+g(x-u_x)\), representing the least cost among all splittings \(x=u+(x-u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution assigns each point the least combined cost over all decompositions into two components; convex component functions produce a convex model.
assumptions_latex: Properness additionally excludes the value \(-\infty\) and requires a finite value somewhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f\mathbin{\square}g)(x)=\inf_u\{f(u)+g(x-u)\}\), and convexity of \(f,g\) implies convexity of \(f\mathbin{\square}g\).

notation.meaning: infimal convolution of f and g

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition and elementary convexity property of infimal convolution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and splitting interpretation fit the leaf, but no source is supplied for the convexity and properness assertions. Source confirmation should also specify the convention when the infimum equals minus infinity.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Value Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex objectives represented as supremal values of parameterized dual expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(Y\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(Q\subseteq Y\) be nonempty, and let \(A:Y\to X\) be linear. Suppose \(\psi:Q\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is finite at some point of \(Q\), and define \(L(x,y)=\langle Ay,x\rangle-\psi(y)\). Then the dual-value objective \(V(x)=\sup_{y\in Q}L(x,y)\) is convex and lower semicontinuous as a pointwise supremum of affine continuous functions of \(x\), and it never takes the value \(-\infty\). When \(Y=X\), \(Q=X\), \(A\) is the identity, and \(\psi=f\), this construction gives \(V=f^*\). The value may equal \(+\infty\) unless its effective domain is restricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking the supremum of expressions affine and continuous in the decision parameter generates a convex lower-semicontinuous value objective, possibly taking positive infinity; Fenchel conjugacy is the identity-map special case.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, \(Y\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space, and \(Q\subseteq Y\) is nonempty.
\(\psi:Q\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is finite at some point of \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(x)=\sup_{y\in Q}\{\langle Ay,x\rangle-\psi(y)\}\) is convex and lower semicontinuous and takes values in \((-infty,+\infty]\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Block-Separable Smooth-Plus-Nonsmooth Composite Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the block-separable specialization of an additive composite objective and its block-gradient notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\ge 1\), let \(\mathbb E=\mathbb E_1\times\cdots\times\mathbb E_p\), and write \(\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_p)\). The block-separable composite model is
\[
\min_{x_i\in\mathbb E_i,\ i=1,\ldots,p} F(\mathbf x),\qquad F(\mathbf x)=f(\mathbf x)+\sum_{i=1}^p g_i(x_i).
\]
Defining
\[
g(\mathbf x)=\sum_{i=1}^p g_i(x_i)
\]
gives \(F=f+g\). Wherever \(f\) is differentiable, its gradient is represented by its block gradients as
\[
\nabla f(\mathbf x)=\bigl(\nabla_1f(\mathbf x),\ldots,\nabla_pf(\mathbf x)\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a product of block spaces, the objective consists of a possibly block-coupled function f and block-separable terms g_i. Their sum is denoted by g. Wherever f is differentiable, its gradient is the tuple of its block gradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
F(\mathbf x)=f(\mathbf x)+g(\mathbf x),\qquad g(\mathbf x)=\sum_{i=1}^p g_i(x_i),\qquad f	ext{ differentiable at }\mathbf x\Rightarrow 
abla f(\mathbf x)=(
abla_1f(\mathbf x),\ldots,
abla_pf(\mathbf x)).
