knowledge_statements.title: Bundle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stabilized finite-cut model used by convex bundle methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be proper closed convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) be the current center, and let \(B=\{(z_i,f(z_i),g_i):g_i\in\partial f(z_i),\ i\in I\}\) be a finite bundle. Its polyhedral model is \[m_B(y)=\max_{i\in I}\{f(z_i)+\langle g_i,y-z_i\rangle\}.\] For a parameter \(t>0\), the proximal bundle trial point is any \[y^+\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{m_B(y)+\frac{1}{2t}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\}.\] Thus the bundle stores function and subgradient information while the quadratic term stabilizes model minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bundle model stores finitely many subgradient cuts and combines their maximum with proximal stabilization to compute a trial point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_B\le f\), with \(y^+\) obtained by stabilized minimization of \(m_B\).

notation.meaning: finite bundle of sampled values and subgradients

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stabilized bundle representation is coherent and correctly scoped to convex bundle models, but no authoritative locator is provided.

children.title: Aggregated-Cut Models
children.top_down_role: Bundle variants compressing multiple cuts into aggregate representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregated-Cut Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex aggregation of affine cuts in a bundle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\ell_i(y)=a_i+\langle g_i,y\rangle\), \(i\in I\), be affine cuts satisfying \(\ell_i(y)\le f(y)\) for all \(y\), and let \(\lambda\) belong to the simplex \(\Delta_I=\{\lambda_i\ge0:\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i=1\}\). The aggregated cut is \[\bar\ell(y)=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i\ell_i(y)=\bar a+\langle\bar g,y\rangle,\qquad \bar a=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i a_i,\quad \bar g=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i g_i.\] It remains a global underestimator: \(\bar\ell(y)\le f(y)\). Consequently, several cuts may be replaced by \(\bar\ell\) without losing their weighted affine information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simplex-weighted combination of valid affine cuts is itself a valid affine cut and can compactly replace stored cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar\ell=\sum_{i\in I}\lambda_i\ell_i\le f\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Convex aggregation preserves the global-cut inequality, but the bundle aggregation interpretation requires an authoritative source.

children.title: Model-Stability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes distinguished by stability of the evolving local approximation.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Stability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratically accurate local-model stability regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), and assign to each \(x\) in a set \(D\subset\operatorname{dom}F\) a local model \(m_x:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). The family is quadratically stable on \(D\) if there exist \(L\ge0\) and \(\rho>0\) such that, for every \(x\in D\), \(m_x(x)=F(x)\), and \[\lvert F(y)-m_x(y)\rvert\le\frac{L}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\] whenever \(y\in D\) and \(\lVert y-x\rVert\le\rho\). This regime separates model error from the stabilization term and makes the local error uniformly second order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model family is quadratically stable when it is exact at every center and has a uniform quadratic approximation error nearby.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_x(x)=F(x)\) and \(\lvert F(y)-m_x(y)\rvert\le(L/2)\lVert y-x\rVert^2\) locally uniformly on \(D\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a coherent quadratic model-accuracy condition, but “model stability” has multiple inequivalent meanings; a source is needed to establish the intended regime.

children.title: Paired Convex Approximation Representation Family
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex models represented through competing convex components or paired directional approximations.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Introduction to Nonsmooth Optimization: Theory, Practice and Software
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Introduction to Nonsmooth Optimization: Theory, Practice and Software

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit DC Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real difference-of-convex representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty convex set. A finite-valued function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) has an explicit difference-of-convex model on \(D\) if two specified proper convex functions \(g,h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) are finite on \(D\) and satisfy \[f(x)=g(x)-h(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in D.\] The ordered pair \((g,h)\) is the supplied DC decomposition. It is part of the model data; different pairs may represent the same function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit DC model supplies two convex functions whose difference equals the modeled function throughout a convex domain.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) and \(h\) are proper convex and finite on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=g-h\) on \(D\), with \((g,h)\) an explicit DC decomposition.

children.title: Composite DC Models
children.top_down_role: DC models embedded in outer-inner composite architectures.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite DC Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit DC model assembled from convex composites and convex regularizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(B:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^q\) be affine, and let \(\phi,r,\psi,s\) be proper convex functions with compatible domains. On any convex set \(D\) where all terms are finite, \[F(x)=\phi(Ax)+r(x)-\psi(Bx)-s(x)\] is a composite DC model. Indeed, defining \(G(x)=\phi(Ax)+r(x)\) and \(H(x)=\psi(Bx)+s(x)\), both \(G\) and \(H\) are convex on \(D\), and \(F=G-H\) there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex functions composed with affine maps, plus convex regularizers, may be grouped into two convex terms forming an explicit composite DC decomposition.
assumptions_latex: All component values are finite on the convex set \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=G-H\) on \(D\), where \(G=\phi\circ A+r\) and \(H=\psi\circ B+s\) are convex.

children.title: Constrained DC Models
children.top_down_role: DC objectives or feasible regions coupled to explicit constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Constrained DC Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DC objective with finitely many DC inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed convex. A constrained DC model has the form \[\min_{x\in C}\;g_0(x)-h_0(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_j(x)-h_j(x)\le0,\qquad j=1,\ldots,m,\] where every \(g_j,h_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper convex and both members of each pair are finite on the relevant part of \(C\). Its feasible set is \(X=\{x\in C:g_j(x)-h_j(x)\le0\text{ for all }j\}\), which need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both the objective and each inequality are represented as differences of convex functions over a closed convex base set.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_j,h_j\) is proper convex and finite where evaluated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X=\{x\in C:g_j(x)-h_j(x)\le0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\), and the objective is \(g_0-h_0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constrained DC formulation is mathematically standard and correctly classified as a definition, but it lacks an inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DC Inequality Sets and Scalar Convex Composite Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of DC feasible sets and reduction of a scalar convex-composite constraint when its zero-sublevel set is a nonempty interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let g_i,h_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be convex for i=1,\ldots,m. A DC inequality set has the form X=\{x\mid g_i(x)-h_i(x)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}. If \varphi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is convex and its zero-sublevel set is the nonempty interval [a,b], where a=-\infty and/or b=+\infty are allowed, then \varphi(g(x)-h(x))\le0 is equivalent to a\le g(x)-h(x)\le b. Each finite endpoint produces a DC inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained DC set is defined by finitely many inequalities between convex differences. When the zero-sublevel set of a scalar convex outer function is a nonempty interval, its composition with g−h is nonpositive exactly when g−h lies in that interval, yielding one or two DC inequalities according to the finite endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi(g(x)-h(x))\le0\iff a\le g(x)-h(x)\le b,\quad\text{and every finite bound is expressible as a DC inequality.}

source_evidence.locator: Stationarity Theory / 6.3. Difference-of-Convex Constraints / Definition 6.3-extra-1

knowledge_statements.title: DC Inequality Sets and Scalar Convex Composite Constraints

children.title: DC Structure Under Composition
children.top_down_role: Preservation or alteration of DC representations through composition.

knowledge_statements.title: DC Structure Under Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine precomposition preserves an explicit DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be convex, let \(f=g-h\) on \(D\), where \(g,h:D\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex, and let \(T(x)=Ax+b\) be affine. On the convex preimage \(E=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:T(x)\in D\}\), \[(f\circ T)(x)=(g\circ T)(x)-(h\circ T)(x).\] Since composition of a convex function with an affine map is convex, \(g\circ T\) and \(h\circ T\) form an explicit DC decomposition of \(f\circ T\) on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precomposing a DC function with an affine map preserves DC structure by composing both convex components with the same map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ T=(g\circ T)-(h\circ T)\) is DC on \(E=T^{-1}(D)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Affine precomposition preserves the displayed DC decomposition, but no source supports this closure property.

children.title: Feasible-Set Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interaction between DC components and constrained feasible geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Set Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real coupling of a finite-valued DC objective and a DC-defined feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(g_j,h_j:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), \(j=0,\ldots,m\), be proper convex functions that are finite on \(C\). Define \(F(x)=g_0(x)-h_0(x)\) for \(x\in C\) and \[X=\{x\in C:g_j(x)-h_j(x)\le 0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}.\] With \(\delta_X(x)=0\) for \(x\in X\) and \(\delta_X(x)=+\infty\) otherwise, the constrained problem is equivalently \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\bigl(F_C(x)+\delta_X(x)\bigr),\] where \(F_C(x)=F(x)\) on \(C\) and \(F_C(x)=+\infty\) outside \(C\). This indicator coupling is exact, although \(\delta_X\) need not be convex when \(X\) is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The feasible-set indicator exactly incorporates the DC constraints into an extended-real objective; this does not make a nonconvex feasible-set indicator convex.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Each \(g_j,h_j\) is proper convex and finite on \(C\).
\(X\) is defined by the stated finite family of DC inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in X}F(x)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{F_C(x)+\delta_X(x)\}\).

notation.meaning: extension of the objective by positive infinity outside the base set

children.title: Diff-Max Models
children.top_down_role: DC models represented through differences involving maximum-type components.

knowledge_statements.title: Diff-Max Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite difference of maxima of convex component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(\{\phi_i\}_{i=1}^p\) and \(\{\psi_j\}_{j=1}^q\) be finite families of convex functions that are finite on \(D\). A diff-max model is \[F(x)=\max_{1\le i\le p}\phi_i(x)-\max_{1\le j\le q}\psi_j(x),\qquad x\in D.\] Each finite maximum is convex, so the displayed formula is an explicit DC decomposition. Nondifferentiability may occur where either maximum has more than one active component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diff-max function subtracts one finite maximum of convex components from another, yielding an explicit DC model with switching surfaces.
assumptions_latex: Every \(\phi_i\) and \(\psi_j\) is convex and finite on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\max_i\phi_i-\max_j\psi_j\) is DC on \(D\).

children.title: Piecewise-DC Models
children.top_down_role: Models whose individual regions admit distinct DC representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-DC Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite regional representation by DC component pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(D_1,\ldots,D_N\subset D\) satisfy \(D=\bigcup_{r=1}^N D_r\), where \(N<\infty\). A function \(F:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is piecewise DC relative to this cover if, for every \(r\), there exist convex functions \(g_r\) and \(h_r\), finite on a convex neighborhood of \(D_r\), such that \[F(x)=g_r(x)-h_r(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in D_r.\] On overlaps, the regional formulas agree because they represent the same single-valued function \(F\). The DC decomposition may change across region boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-DC function has a finite domain cover on each member of which it equals a specified difference of convex functions; regional formulas agree on overlaps.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_r,h_r\) is convex and finite on a convex neighborhood of \(D_r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F|_{D_r}=(g_r-h_r)|_{D_r}\) for every \(r=1,\ldots,N\).

notation.meaning: regional member of the finite cover

children.title: Max-Component Switching
children.top_down_role: Switching geometry induced by competing maximum components.

knowledge_statements.title: Max-Component Switching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-index switching in a finite difference-of-max representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\max_{i\in I}g_i(x)-\max_{j\in J}h_j(x)\), where \(I,J\) are finite and every component is continuous. Define \(I(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{i\in I}g_i(x)\) and \(J(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{j\in J}h_j(x)\). On any open set where \(I(x)=\{i\}\) and \(J(x)=\{j\}\), one has \(f=g_i-h_j\). Hence a change of the local DC formula can occur only where at least one active set is non-singleton; equivalently, where two components of the corresponding maximum tie.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A difference-of-max model equals one component difference wherever both maxima have unique active indices; formula switching occurs only at component ties.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i\) and \(h_j\) is continuous on a common domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(x)=\{i\},\ J(x)=\{j\}\Rightarrow f=g_i-h_j\) locally, and switching requires \(|I(x)|>1\) or \(|J(x)|>1\).

notation.meaning: active index sets of the two maxima

children.title: DC Partition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Interfaces between regions carrying different DC pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: DC Partition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundaries of active-component cells in a finite diff-max model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\max_{i\in I}g_i(x)-\max_{j\in J}h_j(x)\), define the strict active cell \(C_{ij}=\{x:g_i(x)>g_k(x)\ \forall k\ne i,\ h_j(x)>h_\ell(x)\ \forall \ell\ne j\}\). The DC partition boundary is \(B=\operatorname{dom}f\setminus\bigcup_{i,j}C_{ij}\). Equivalently, \(B\) consists of points where at least one maximum has multiple active components. If the components are continuous, every \(C_{ij}\) is relatively open and \(f=g_i-h_j\) on \(C_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The partition boundary is the set where either component maximum has a tie; away from it, one fixed DC component formula applies.
assumptions_latex: All component functions are continuous on \(\operatorname{dom}f\).

notation.meaning: strict cell with uniquely active components i and j

knowledge_statements.title: DC Decomposition Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic nonuniqueness of a difference-of-convex decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and suppose \(f=g-h\) on \(C\), with \(g,h:C\to\mathbb{R}\) convex. For every convex function \(q:C\to\mathbb{R}\), \[f=(g+q)-(h+q).\] Thus a DC function generally has infinitely many decompositions; taking \(q\) from any infinite family of distinct finite convex functions produces distinct pairs. Consequently, decomposition-dependent quantities, such as chosen component subgradients or curvature bounds, are not intrinsic to \(f\) unless a decomposition is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the same convex function to both DC components leaves their difference unchanged, so DC decompositions and component-based quantities are generally nonunique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=(g+q)-(h+q)\) for every finite convex \(q:C\to\mathbb{R}\).

notation.meaning: a common convex perturbation of both DC components

children.title: Quasidifferentiable Models
children.top_down_role: Models organized through paired directional approximation structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasidifferentiable Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional directional-derivative definition using a quasidifferential pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is quasidifferentiable at \(x\) if it is directionally differentiable there and there exist nonempty compact convex sets \(\underline{\partial}f(x),\overline{\partial}f(x)\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) such that, for every direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[f'(x;d)=\max_{u\in\underline{\partial}f(x)}\langle u,d\rangle+\min_{v\in\overline{\partial}f(x)}\langle v,d\rangle.\] The ordered pair \((\underline{\partial}f(x),\overline{\partial}f(x))\) is a quasidifferential of \(f\) at \(x\) and is generally nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model is quasidifferentiable when every directional derivative is the sum of a support minimum and support maximum generated by compact convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;\cdot)\) admits the displayed max-plus-min representation by two nonempty compact convex sets.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed max-plus-min definition is a standard finite-dimensional quasidifferential convention, but no inspectable source establishes the convention or the nonuniqueness assertion. The plain text should say maximum plus minimum of linear forms, rather than “support minimum.”

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local convexity implies membership in M(x)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient local-convexity condition for membership in the source-defined class M(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is convex in some convex neighborhood of \(x\), then \(f\in M(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If f is convex in some convex neighborhood of x, then f belongs to the source-defined class M(x).
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is convex in some convex neighborhood of }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in M(x)

source_evidence.locator: Quasidifferentiable functions / III.4. Relationship between the quasidifferential and the subdifferentials of Penot and Clarke / Proposition 4.3

children.title: Quasi-DC Models
children.top_down_role: Models possessing local or generalized DC-like representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-DC Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional quasi-DC sense; terminology requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A directionally differentiable function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is directionally quasi-DC at \(x\) if there exist finite continuous sublinear functions \(p_x,q_x:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \[f'(x;d)=p_x(d)-q_x(d)\qquad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] Equivalently in finite dimensions, there are nonempty compact convex sets \(A_x,B_x\) with \(p_x=\sigma_{A_x}\) and \(q_x=\sigma_{B_x}\). This pointwise directional property does not by itself assert that \(f\) is locally a difference of convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directional quasi-DC model has each directional derivative representable as a difference of two finite sublinear support functions, without requiring a local DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;\cdot)=p_x-q_x=\sigma_{A_x}-\sigma_{B_x}\).

notation.meaning: support function of the set A

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The difference-of-sublinear-functions representation is mathematically meaningful, but “directionally quasi-DC” is not standardized sufficiently to confirm that it denotes the exact class intended by this leaf without an authoritative source.

children.title: Paired Directional Approximations
children.top_down_role: Directional model structure expressed through paired convex components.

knowledge_statements.title: Paired Directional Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent max-plus-min and difference-of-support representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty compact convex sets. The paired directional approximation generated by \((A,B)\) is \[m(d)=\max_{a\in A}\langle a,d\rangle+\min_{b\in B}\langle b,d\rangle=\sigma_A(d)-\sigma_{-B}(d).\] Thus the first component is sublinear and the second displayed minimum is superlinear. A directionally differentiable function has this approximation at \(x\) precisely when \(f'(x;d)=m(d)\) for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact convex pair generates a directional model expressible equivalently as max plus min or as a difference of support functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m=\sigma_A-\sigma_{-B}\), and \(m=f'(x;\cdot)\) exactly when the pair represents the directional derivative.

notation.meaning: support function, equal to the maximum of the inner product over A

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The identity between the max-plus-min form and the difference-of-support-functions form is correct, and representation is the appropriate content kind. An authoritative source with a specific locator is nevertheless required for this quasidifferential representation record.

children.title: Representation Gap Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes separating quasidifferential structure from usable quasi-DC structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Gap Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition separating pointwise directional pairs from local DC representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be directionally differentiable on an open set \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), with \(f'(x;\cdot)=p_x-q_x\) for each \(x\in U\), where \(p_x,q_x\) are sublinear. The pair field is locally DC-integrable at \(\bar x\) if some neighborhood \(V\subset U\) and finite convex functions \(g,h\) on \(V\) satisfy \(f=g-h\) and \(g'(x;\cdot)=p_x\), \(h'(x;\cdot)=q_x\) for all \(x\in V\). A representation-gap regime occurs when pointwise pairs exist but this compatibility condition fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The representation gap is present when directional DC pairs exist pointwise but cannot be integrated into one pair of convex functions on a neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\) is in the gap regime exactly when pointwise decompositions exist near \(\bar x\) but no compatible local convex pair \((g,h)\) exists.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record introduces a coherent compatibility condition, but neither “locally DC-integrable” nor “representation-gap regime” is sourced as a recognized convention. A source is needed to determine whether this is the intended mathematical boundary rather than a newly coined definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Codifferentiable Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional codifferentiability via paired convex compact affine models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is codifferentiable at \(x\) if there exist nonempty compact convex sets \(\underline d f(x),\overline d f(x)\subset\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^n\), normalized so that the maximum and minimum of their scalar coordinates are zero, and \[f(x+h)-f(x)=\max_{(a,v)\in\underline d f(x)}(a+\langle v,h\rangle)+\min_{(b,w)\in\overline d f(x)}(b+\langle w,h\rangle)+o(\|h\|).\] The ordered pair is a codifferential of \(f\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A codifferentiable model has a first-order increment equal to paired maxima and minima of affine functions, up to a little-o remainder.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The increment of \(f\) admits the displayed paired affine approximation with remainder \(o(\|h\|)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The paired affine little-o model resembles the standard finite-dimensional codifferential definition, but the precise normalization and codifferential convention require an authoritative cited definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional uniform and continuous codifferentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity refinements of codifferentiability, together with the function classes explicitly stated to admit Hausdorff-continuous codifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, \(x\in X\), and let \(f\) be finite on \(X\). The function \(f\) is directionally uniformly codifferentiable at \(x\) if the codifferential remainder satisfies \[\frac{o_x(\alpha\Delta)}{\alpha}\to0\quad\text{as }\alpha\downarrow0\] uniformly with respect to \(\Delta\in S_1\), where \(S_1\) is the unit sphere. It is continuously codifferentiable at \(x\) if it is codifferentiable in a neighborhood of \(x\) and the mappings \(y\mapsto\underline d f(y)\) and \(y\mapsto\bar d f(y)\) are Hausdorff continuous at \(x\). Functions admitting Hausdorff-continuous codifferentials include nonsmooth convex functions, nonsmooth concave functions, and functions represented as a max–min of finitely many smooth functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional uniform codifferentiability requires the normalized codifferential remainder to converge to zero uniformly over unit directions. Continuous codifferentiability requires local codifferentiability and Hausdorff continuity at the point of both codifferential components. Nonsmooth convex and concave functions and finite max-min representations of smooth functions are included among functions admitting Hausdorff-continuous codifferentials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{o_x(\alpha\Delta)}{\alpha}\to0\text{ uniformly for }\Delta\in S_1\text{ defines directional uniform codifferentiability, while local codifferentiability and Hausdorff continuity of both component mappings define continuous codifferentiability at }x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise equivalence of codifferentiability and quasidifferentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality of the two pointwise nonsmooth function classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a function \(f\) and a point \(x\), \(f\) is codifferentiable at \(x\) if and only if \(f\) is quasidifferentiable at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The functions codifferentiable at a given point are exactly the functions quasidifferentiable at that point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Codifferentiability and its principal variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise codifferentiability via paired compact convex affine models, together with uniform, continuous, hypo-, and hyperdifferentiable variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open, \(x\in X\), and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be finite. The function \(f\) is codifferentiable at \(x\) if there exist compact convex sets \(\underline d f(x),\overline d f(x)\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\) such that, for every \(\Delta\) satisfying \(\operatorname{co}\{x,x+\Delta\}\subset X\),
\[
f(x+\Delta)=f(x)+\Phi_x(\Delta)+o_x(\Delta),
\]
where
\[
\Phi_x(\Delta)=\max_{[a,v]\in\underline d f(x)}\bigl(a+\langle v,\Delta\rangle\bigr)+\min_{[b,w]\in\overline d f(x)}\bigl(b+\langle w,\Delta\rangle\bigr)
\]
and, for every direction \(\Delta\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
\frac{o_x(\alpha\Delta)}{\alpha}\to0\qquad(\alpha\downarrow0).
\]
The pair \(Df(x)=[\underline d f(x),\overline d f(x)]\) is a codifferential, whose two components are the hypodifferential and hyperdifferential; it need not be unique. Codifferentiability is uniform in directions when the remainder limit is uniform over \(\|\Delta\|=1\). The function is continuously codifferentiable at \(x\) when it is codifferentiable near \(x\) and admits a codifferential mapping that is Hausdorff-continuous at \(x\). It is hypodifferentiable at \(x\) if a codifferential can be chosen with \(\overline d f(x)=\{0_{n+1}\}\), and hyperdifferentiable at \(x\) if one can be chosen with \(\underline d f(x)=\{0_{n+1}\}\). The associated first-order model is \(F_x(\Delta)=f(x)+\Phi_x(\Delta)\), with uniform directional approximation under the uniform condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite function on an open subset of Euclidean space is codifferentiable at a point when its increment has a first-order model consisting of a maximum of affine functions plus a minimum of affine functions, generated by two compact convex sets, with a directionwise little-o remainder. The definition also yields uniform, continuous, hypo-, and hyperdifferentiable variants. A codifferential is generally nonunique and supplies the stated first-order model.
assumptions_latex: X\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is open},\quad x\in X
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,\underline d f(x),\overline d f(x)\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}\text{ compact and convex such that }f(x+\Delta)-f(x)=\max_{[a,v]\in\underline d f(x)}(a+\langle v,\Delta\rangle)+\min_{[b,w]\in\overline d f(x)}(b+\langle w,\Delta\rangle)+o_x(\Delta),\quad \frac{o_x(\alpha\Delta)}{\alpha}\to0\ (\alpha\downarrow0).

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Convex–Concave Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit saddle-value realization of a nonsmooth model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty set, let \(Y\) and \(Z\) be nonempty compact convex subsets of finite-dimensional real vector spaces, and let \(\Phi:X\times Y\times Z\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous in \((y,z)\) for each fixed \(x\in X\), convex in \(y\) for fixed \((x,z)\), and concave in \(z\) for fixed \((x,y)\). The implicit convex–concave saddle-value model generated by \(\Phi\) is \[f(x)=\min_{y\in Y}\max_{z\in Z}\Phi(x,y,z)=\max_{z\in Z}\min_{y\in Y}\Phi(x,y,z),\qquad x\in X.\] The resulting value function can be nonsmooth where its optimizing sets change with \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implicit convex–concave model represents the objective as the common minimax and maximin saddle value of a continuous convex–concave generating function; changes in optimizers can produce nonsmoothness.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) and \(Z\) are nonempty compact convex subsets of finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
For each \(x\in X\), the function \(\Phi(x,\cdot,\cdot)\) is continuous, convex in its \(Y\)-variable, and concave in its \(Z\)-variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in X\), \(f(x)=\min_{y\in Y}\max_{z\in Z}\Phi(x,y,z)=\max_{z\in Z}\min_{y\in Y}\Phi(x,y,z)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Partly Smooth Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial smoothness relative to an active manifold in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper lower-semicontinuous function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is partly smooth at \(\bar x\) relative to a \(C^2\) manifold \(M\) containing \(\bar x\) if: \(f|_M\) is \(C^2\) near \(\bar x\); \(f\) is subdifferentially regular along \(M\) near \(\bar x\); the mapping \(x\mapsto\partial f(x)\) is continuous at \(\bar x\) relative to \(M\); and the sharpness identity \[\operatorname{par}(\partial f(\bar x))=N_M(\bar x)\] holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partly smooth function is smooth along an active manifold, regular and subdifferentially continuous there, with nonsmooth directions exactly normal to that manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Smoothness, regularity, relative subdifferential continuity, and \(\operatorname{par}(\partial f(\bar x))=N_M(\bar x)\) characterize partial smoothness.

knowledge_statements.title: Definable Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real functions definable in a fixed o-minimal structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an o-minimal structure \(\mathcal O=(\mathcal O_n)_{n\ge 1}\) over the real field. A set \(S\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is definable if \(S\in\mathcal O_n\). An extended-real function \(f:D	o(-\infty,+\infty]\) is definable if its domain and finite graph \[\{(x,r)\in D\times\mathbb{R}:f(x)=r<+\infty\}\] are definable; equivalently, under the usual encoding of \(+\infty\), its epigraph is definable. Such a function admits finite definable stratifications locally on bounded sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A definable model is one whose domain and graph belong to a fixed o-minimal structure; it consequently admits tame local stratifications.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal O\) is a fixed o-minimal expansion of the real field.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is definable exactly when its domain and finite graph are definable in \(\mathcal O\).

notation.meaning: family of definable subsets of n-dimensional real space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-graph definition is plausible for an extended-real definable function, but the asserted epigraph equivalence depends on how +∞ values are encoded, and the stratification consequence needs a specific o-minimal source.

children.title: Tame Stratification Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Connections between definable geometry and stratified model structure.

assumptions_latex: A neighborhood of \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) in \(\operatorname{gph}f\) admits a finite \(C^1\) Whitney stratification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The compatible domain strata provide smooth interfaces for identifying active manifolds near \(\bar x\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Whitney-compatible graph strata are the standard interface between tame geometry and local smooth active-manifold analysis.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local interface between graph stratifications and smooth active pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tame stratification interface for \(f\) at \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) is a finite \(C^1\) Whitney stratification \(\{S_i\}_{i=1}^N\) of \(\operatorname{gph}f\) near \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) such that each restriction \(\pi_x|_{S_i}\) has constant rank. The projected pieces \(M_i=\pi_x(S_i)\) are required to be embedded \(C^1\) manifolds, and \(f|_{M_i}\) is \(C^1\) wherever \(\pi_x|_{S_i}\) is locally one-to-one. A stratum containing \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) thereby determines a candidate active manifold through \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tame interface decomposes the local graph into compatible smooth strata whose domain projections supply candidate active manifolds.
knowledge_statements.title: Tame Stratification Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed interface is plausible, but “tame stratification interface” is not established as a standard definition, and constant-rank graph projections alone do not certify active-manifold identification. A source must specify the required stratification and identification hypotheses.

children.title: Nondefinable Boundary Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric regimes outside the selected tame category.

assumptions_latex: The ambient structure is an arbitrary o-minimal expansion of the ordered real field.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graph of \(g\) is not definable in any o-minimal expansion of the ordered real field.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: o-minimal subsets of the real line have finitely many connected components, excluding an accumulating sequence of isolated zeros.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete oscillatory boundary beyond o-minimal definability; stratifiability in broader categories is not excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(g(0)=0\) and \(g(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)\) for \(x\ne0\). Its zero set contains \(x_k=(k\pi)^{-1/2}\) for every positive integer \(k\), and these isolated zeros accumulate at \(0\). If \(g\) were definable in an o-minimal expansion of the ordered real field, then \(Z(g)=\{x:g(x)=0\}\) would be a definable subset of \(\mathbb{R}\), hence a finite union of points and intervals. The accumulating isolated sequence contradicts that conclusion, so this continuous nonsmooth-model source lies beyond the definable regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinitely oscillating continuous function has isolated zeros accumulating at zero, which is impossible for a definable subset of the real line.
knowledge_statements.title: Nondefinable Boundary Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oscillatory-zero argument is mathematically plausible and fits the failure-boundary container, but the universal claim covering every o-minimal expansion requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

assumptions_latex: \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\), where \(\partial f\) is a specified limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without local uniqueness, smooth restriction, and subdifferential continuity, no identifiable active-manifold model is certified at \(\bar x\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: active-manifold identification requires a locally coherent smooth stratum and stable subdifferential behavior.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure predicate relative to partial smoothness and local manifold identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Active-manifold identification fails at \(\bar x\) whenever every embedded \(C^1\) manifold \(M\) through \(\bar x\) violates at least one required interface property: \(f|_M\) is not \(C^1\) near \(\bar x\); the mapping \(x\mapsto\partial f(x)\) restricted to \(M\) is not continuous at \(\bar x\); the sharpness relation \(\operatorname{par}(\partial f(\bar x))=N_M(\bar x)\) fails; or nearby points with comparable function values and subgradients approaching \(0\) do not eventually lie in \(M\). Such branching, oscillation, or degeneracy prevents a stable smooth active reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Active-manifold reduction fails when no local smooth piece simultaneously supports smooth restriction, subdifferential continuity, sharpness, and identification.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Manifold Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record blends partial smoothness, identifiability, and a sequence-based identification condition without fixing a sourced definition. A source is needed to determine which properties are necessary for the intended active-manifold notion.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is Clarke pseudoconvex on \(C\) if, for every \(x,y\in C\), the strict decrease condition \(f(y)<f(x)\) implies \(f^{\circ}(x;y-x)<0\), where \[f^{\circ}(x;d)=\limsup_{\substack{z\to x\\ t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(z+td)-f(z)}{t}.\] Equivalently, because \(f^{\circ}(x;d)=\max_{v\in\partial_C f(x)}\langle v,d\rangle\), strict decrease from \(x\) toward \(y\) forces every Clarke subgradient \(v\in\partial_C f(x)\) to satisfy \(\langle v,y-x\rangle<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz function is Clarke pseudoconvex when every point with lower value gives a strictly negative Clarke directional derivative.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every interior point of a line segment, a generalized pseudoconvex function is no larger than the greater endpoint value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(z)\leq\max\{f(x),f(y)\}

children.title: Invex Models
children.top_down_role: Generalized-convexity models organized by an invex mapping structure.

assumptions_latex: \(\eta:C\times C\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is a prescribed displacement map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is invex when \(f(y)-f(x)\ge\langle\nabla f(x),\eta(y,x)\rangle\) for all \(x,y\in C\).

notation.meaning: invex displacement map from x toward y

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the gradient inequality with a displacement map is the standard differentiable definition of an invex function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable scalar invexity with a fixed displacement map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is invex on \(C\) with respect to \(\eta\) if \[f(y)-f(x)\ge \langle\nabla f(x),\eta(y,x)\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in C.\] The pair \((C,\eta)\) is part of the model specification; changing \(\eta\) changes the invexity claim. Ordinary differentiable convexity is recovered by taking \(\eta(y,x)=y-x\) on a convex set \(C\). Under this definition, any stationary point \(x\in C\) satisfying \(\nabla f(x)=0\) is a global minimizer of \(f\) on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invex model replaces the convex displacement by a prescribed map while retaining a global first-order lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Invex Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The differentiable invexity inequality and stationary-point consequence are standard and fit the container, but no inspectable citation or locator supports the record.

children.title: Preinvex Models
children.top_down_role: Generalized-convexity models organized along invex paths.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty and invex with respect to \(\eta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is preinvex when \(f(x+t\eta(y,x))\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\) for all admissible \(x,y,t\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Jensen convexity along eta-generated paths is the standard definition of preinvexity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar preinvexity along affine-in-parameter paths generated by a displacement map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(C\) is invex with respect to \(\eta:C\times C\to\mathbb{R}^n\) when \(x+t\eta(y,x)\in C\) for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). On such a set, \(f\) is preinvex with respect to \(\eta\) if \[f(x+t\eta(y,x))\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C,
\ t\in[0,1].\] With \(\eta(y,x)=y-x\), this reduces to ordinary convexity. Unlike differentiable invexity, the definition does not require derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A preinvex function satisfies the convex interpolation inequality along paths generated by a prescribed displacement map.
knowledge_statements.title: Preinvex Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of an invex set and the preinvex interpolation inequality are mathematically coherent and container-appropriate, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Path-Dependent Generalized Convexity
children.top_down_role: Generalized-convexity behavior determined by admissible connecting paths.

assumptions_latex: For every \(x,y\in C\), a path \(\gamma_{x,y}:[0,1]\to C\) is prescribed with \(\gamma_{x,y}(0)=x\) and \(\gamma_{x,y}(1)=y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Generalized convexity is evaluated along the specified family \(\{\gamma_{x,y}\}\), so it depends on both \(f\) and the path geometry.

notation.meaning: prescribed path from x to y

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pathwise Jensen inequalities provide the common geometric form underlying preinvex and geodesically convex models.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract pathwise formulation encompassing preinvex and geodesic convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Relative to the prescribed path family, \(f:C\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is path-convex if \[f(\gamma_{x,y}(t))\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C,
\ t\in[0,1].\] It is path-quasiconvex if the right-hand side is replaced by \(\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\). Preinvexity is the special case \(\gamma_{x,y}(t)=x+t\eta(y,x)\), while geodesic convexity uses selected geodesics. Thus the generalized-convexity class is not a property of \(f\) alone; it is relative to the admissible connecting paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Path-dependent convexity imposes convex or quasiconvex interpolation along a specified family of connecting paths rather than necessarily along line segments.
knowledge_statements.title: Path-Dependent Generalized Convexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract pathwise formulation fits the container, but the admissible path-family assumptions and the relationship to geodesic convexity require a source fixing the intended generality.

children.title: Invexity Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where the relevant invex structure does not support the model geometry.

assumptions_latex: Invexity is interpreted by the differentiable gradient inequality for some map \(\eta:C\times C\to\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No displacement map \(\eta\) can make \(f(x)=x^3\) invex on \(\mathbb{R}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: differentiable invexity forces every stationary point to be globally minimizing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationary nonminimum as a sharp obstruction to differentiable invexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=x^3\), one has \(f'(0)=0\), but \(0\) is not a global minimizer because \(f(y)<f(0)=0\) whenever \(y<0\). If \(f\) were invex with respect to some \(\eta\), its defining inequality at \(x=0\) would give \[f(y)-f(0)\ge f'(0)\eta(y,0)=0\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb{R}.\] This contradicts \(f(y)<0\) for \(y<0\). Hence a differentiable function possessing a stationary point that is not globally minimizing lies outside every invex model of this form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cubic function cannot be invex under any displacement map because its stationary point at zero is not a global minimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Invexity Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cubic is a valid obstruction under the stated differentiable invexity inequality, and counterexample is an appropriate kind for this failure container. No inspectable source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Singular Discontinuous Model Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Singular, discontinuous, nonclosed, and nonattaining models outside standard locally Lipschitz regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The penalty \(P_p\) is continuous and nonconvex but is not locally Lipschitz at any point having a zero component.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: scalar powers with exponent between zero and one have unbounded slope at the origin and approximate support counting pointwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional non-Lipschitz power penalties used as continuous sparsity surrogates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The singular power penalty is \[P_p(x)=\lambda\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|^p.\] It is finite and continuous on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), smooth where every component is nonzero, and nonconvex for \(0<p<1\). Since \(|t|^p/|t|=|t|^{p-1}\to+\infty\) as \(t\to0\), \(P_p\) is not locally Lipschitz at points with a zero component. Moreover, for fixed \(x\), \[\lim_{p\downarrow0}\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|^p=\|x\|_0=|\operatorname{supp}(x)|,\] so these penalties approach cardinality counting pointwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fractional power penalties continuously approximate support counting but are nonconvex and have singular, non-Lipschitz behavior at zero components.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Sparsity Penalties

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The continuity, nonconvexity, non-Lipschitz behavior, and pointwise cardinality limit are coherent and appropriate properties of singular sparsity penalties, but they lack a cited source.

children.title: Rank Models
children.top_down_role: Matrix-valued models driven by rank selection or rank penalties.

assumptions_latex: Any additional loss \(\ell:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rank penalization and rank constraints encode selection of the number of nonzero singular values.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: matrix rank equals the number of positive singular values and yields standard penalized or constrained low-rank models.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional matrix rank as a discontinuous spectral selection model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q=\min\{m,n\}\), matrix rank has the spectral counting representation \[\operatorname{rank}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{q}\mathbf{1}_{(0,\infty)}(\sigma_i(X)).\] A rank-penalized model therefore has the form \[\min_{X\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}}\ \ell(X)+\lambda\operatorname{rank}(X),\qquad \lambda>0,\] while a rank-constrained model imposes \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\le r\). The rank function is integer-valued and lower semicontinuous but discontinuous at every matrix whose rank can increase under arbitrarily small perturbations, in particular at every rank-deficient matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix rank counts positive singular values and produces either a discontinuous rank penalty or a low-rank feasibility constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The spectral counting representation and the stated lower-semicontinuity and discontinuity behavior of rank are correct in finite dimensions and fit the representation container, but no source is cited.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hard and soft low-rank matrix formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact representations of a prescribed rank bound and spectral-penalty formulations for promoting low rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(1\le r\le n\le m\), \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), \(\|Z\|_{(r)}=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i(Z)\), and \(\|Z\|_*=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i(Z)\). Then \(\operatorname{rank}(Z)\le r\iff \sum_{i=r+1}^n\sigma_i(Z)=0\iff \|Z\|_*-\|Z\|_{(r)}=0\), where the last equality is a difference-of-convex equation. Also, \(\operatorname{rank}(Z)\le r\iff Z=UV\) for some \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\) and \(V\in\mathbb R^{r\times m}\). For symmetric \(Z\), the equality may equivalently be expressed using its ordered absolute eigenvalues. Thus a hard model minimizes \(f(Z)\) over \(Z\in\mathcal Z\) subject to this rank bound, whereas a soft model has the form \(\min_{Z\in\mathcal Z} f(Z)+\gamma P(Z)\). An absolutely symmetric \(p:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) induces \(P(Z)=p(\sigma(Z))\); a symmetric \(p\) induces \(P(Z)=p(\lambda(Z))\) on \(\mathbb S^n\). The cited DC sparsity surrogates satisfying the stated surrogate conditions induce DC low-rank spectral surrogates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prescribed matrix-rank bound has exact nuclear-minus-Ky-Fan and low-dimensional factorization representations. When rank is not prescribed, low rank may instead be promoted by a spectral penalty generated from singular values or, for symmetric matrices, eigenvalues. The cited qualified DC sparsity surrogates yield DC spectral low-rank surrogates.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal Z\subseteq\mathbb R^{n\times m}\text{ is closed for the optimization models}
f:\mathbb R^{n\times m}\to\mathbb R\text{ may be nonconvex and nondifferentiable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rank}(Z)\le r\iff \|Z\|_*-\|Z\|_{(r)}=0\iff (\exists U\in\mathbb R^{n\times r})(\exists V\in\mathbb R^{r\times m})\ Z=UV.

children.title: Cardinality Models
children.top_down_role: Vector-valued models driven by support-size counting.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cardinality models select supports by penalizing or constraining \(\|x\|_0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the ell-zero functional is exactly the support cardinality and defines standard sparse penalized and constrained models.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional support selection through the discontinuous cardinality functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The cardinality functional is \[\|x\|_0=|\operatorname{supp}(x)|=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}}(x_i),\qquad \operatorname{supp}(x)=\{i:x_i\ne0\}.\] A cardinality-penalized model has the form \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\ \ell(x)+\lambda\|x\|_0,
\qquad \lambda>0,\] and a cardinality-constrained model imposes \(\|x\|_0\le s\). The functional is integer-valued and lower semicontinuous, but it is discontinuous at every vector with at least one zero component because an arbitrarily small perturbation can activate that component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cardinality models count nonzero coordinates and encode sparse selection through an ell-zero penalty or a support-size constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The support-counting representation and the penalized and constrained formulations are coherent and fit the cardinality-model container, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Matrix Selection Structure
children.top_down_role: Low-dimensional matrix selection expressed through rank-sensitive objectives.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(AS(z)\) contains exactly the selected columns of \(A\), with unselected columns replaced by zero, and \(\operatorname{rank}(AS(z))\leq \|z\|_0\leq k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary diagonal selection for column-structured rank-cardinality models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), a column-selection structure is represented by \(z\in\{0,1\}^n\) and \(S(z)=\operatorname{Diag}(z)\). The selected matrix is \(AS(z)\), and a budget of at most \(k\) selected columns is imposed by \(\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}z=\|z\|_0\leq k\). Consequently, every nonzero column of \(AS(z)\) corresponds to an index \(j\) with \(z_j=1\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(AS(z))\leq\|z\|_0\leq k\). Row selection is obtained analogously by left multiplication with a binary diagonal matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary diagonal matrix selects columns of a matrix; a cardinality budget bounds both the number of retained columns and the selected matrix's rank.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Selection Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and rank bound are mathematically correct and fit the matrix-selection leaf, but no inspectable source supports the chosen column-selection convention.

children.title: Support-Counting Discontinuities
children.top_down_role: Discontinuities caused by changes in the number of nonzero components.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Counting Discontinuities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional discontinuity structure of the cardinality function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(s:\mathbb{R}^n\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\) by \(s(x)=\|x\|_0=|\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i\neq0\}|\). The function \(s\) is discontinuous at every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) having at least one zero coordinate and is locally constant at every \(x\) whose coordinates are all nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support count is discontinuous exactly at vectors having a zero coordinate and is locally constant where every coordinate is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\) is discontinuous at every point having a zero coordinate and locally constant where all coordinates are nonzero.
\(f\) is nonclosed exactly when \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is not closed, equivalently when \(f\) is not lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional epigraphical closedness and its open-set failure example.

source_refs.locator: A. Convex Sets and Functions p. 38

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A proper extended-valued function \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is closed when its epigraph \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,
obreak\alpha)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is closed; in finite dimensions this is equivalent to lower semicontinuity. Thus a nonclosed model admits \(x_k\to x\) with \(\liminf_k f(x_k)<f(x)\). Concretely, if \(C\subset X\) is nonempty and not closed, its indicator \(\delta_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise is nonclosed: for \(x_k\in C\) converging to \(x\in\overline C\setminus C\), one has \(\delta_C(x_k)=0\) but \(\delta_C(x)=+
obreak\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-valued model is nonclosed when its epigraph is not closed. The indicator of any nonclosed feasible set is a canonical example.

children.title: Recession-Driven Failures
children.top_down_role: Proximal pathologies associated with unfavorable recession behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Driven Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A pathwise sufficient condition for recession-driven proximal failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y(t)=y_0+td\), where \(d\neq0\), and suppose \(y(t)\in\operatorname{dom}f\) for all sufficiently large \(t\). If \[\liminf_{t\to\infty}\frac{f(y_0+td)}{t^2}< -\frac{\|d\|^2}{2\lambda},\] then \(\inf_y Q_{\lambda,x}(y)=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a function decreases along an unbounded ray faster than the proximal quadratic grows, the proximal subproblem is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_y Q_{\lambda,x}(y)=-\infty\).

children.title: Infimum-Escape Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nonattainment regimes where minimizing sequences escape bounded regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Infimum-Escape Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of finite, unattained infima by minimizing-sequence behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_*=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}Q(y)\in\mathbb{R}\), suppose \(\operatorname*{argmin}Q=\varnothing\), and let \((y_k)\) satisfy \(Q(y_k)\to q_*\). Then either \((y_k)\) eventually leaves every bounded subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\), or it has a subsequence converging to some \(\bar y\) at which lower semicontinuity fails, with \(Q(\bar y)>q_*\). In particular, if \(Q\) is lower semicontinuous, every minimizing sequence eventually leaves every bounded set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite unattained infimum, each minimizing sequence either escapes every bounded set or has a cluster point witnessing failure of lower semicontinuity; under lower semicontinuity only escape is possible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every minimizing sequence either eventually leaves every bounded set or has a convergent subsequence whose limit witnesses failure of lower semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear-Program Value Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued value function of a parameterized nonlinear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each parameter \(x\in X\), define \(S(x)=\{y\in Y:g_i(x,y)\leq0,\ i=1,\ldots,p\}\). The nonlinear-program value function is \[v(x)=\inf_{y\in S(x)}F(x,y).\] The convention is \(v(x)=+\infty\) when \(S(x)=\varnothing\) and \(v(x)=-\infty\) when \(F(x,\cdot)\) is unbounded below on \(S(x)\). When the infimum is finite and attained, \(M(x)=\{y\in S(x):F(x,y)=v(x)\}\). Even when \(F\) and \(g\) are smooth, changes in active constraints or minimizers can make \(v\) nonsmooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a parameterized nonlinear objective over parameter-dependent constraints produces an extended-valued value function that may be nonsmooth even when all input functions are smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parametric nonlinear program induces the extended-valued marginal function \(v(x)=\inf_{y\in S(x)}F(x,y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential representation of a convex parametric optimal-value function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier-based subdifferential formula for a parametric nonlinear-program value function; the inherited assumptions of Corollary 4.6 remain unresolved in this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the assumptions of Corollary 4.6, suppose that \(f\) and \(g_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,p\), are jointly convex in \((x,y)\), and that \(h_j\), \(j=1,\ldots,q\), are affine in \((x,y)\). Then
\[
\partial\varphi(y^0)=\bigcup_{(\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda(x^0,y^0)}\nabla_yL(x^0,y^0,\lambda,\mu).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the inherited assumptions of Corollary 4.6, if the objective and inequality functions are jointly convex in the decision and parameter variables and the equality functions are affine in those variables, then the value-function subdifferential at the parameter equals the union of the parameter gradients of the Lagrangian over the associated multiplier set.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ and }g_i\ (i=1,\ldots,p)\text{ are jointly convex in }(x,y).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\varphi(y^0)=\bigcup_{(\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda(x^0,y^0)}\nabla_yL(x^0,y^0,\lambda,\mu).

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Program Value Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inequality-constrained parametric quadratic-program value representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each parameter \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define \[v(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}\left\{\frac12y^{\mathsf T}Q(x)y+c(x)^{\mathsf T}y:A(x)y\leq b(x)\right\}.\] The value is \(+\infty\) when the constraint system is infeasible and \(-\infty\) when the quadratic objective is unbounded below on the feasible set. When the value is finite and attained, \(M(x)\) is the set of feasible points attaining \(v(x)\). Parameter-dependent active sets, degeneracy, or changes in \(M(x)\) can make \(v\) nonsmooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parametric quadratic program maps each parameter to its optimal quadratic objective value, with extended values representing infeasibility or unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The parameterized quadratic program defines an extended-valued marginal function through its optimal objective value.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-domain characterization for a biparameterized quadratic program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes finiteness of the optimal value for the right-hand-side and linear-objective parameterization under copositivity on the recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and define \(A_\infty:=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:Av\ge 0\}\) and \(\mathcal P_A(b):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\ge b\}\). Suppose that \(Q\) is copositive on \(A_\infty\). Then
\[
(b,c)\in\operatorname{dom}(Q,A)
\iff
\mathcal P_A(b)\ne\varnothing
\ \text{and}\ 
\forall(x,v,\eta),\quad
\left.
\begin{aligned}
Qv-A^\top\eta&=0,\\
0\le\eta&\perp Av\ge0,\\
Ax&\ge b
\end{aligned}
\right\}
\Longrightarrow (c+Qx)^\top v\ge0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed symmetric Q and A, assume Q is copositive on the recession cone {v: Av ≥ 0}. A parameter pair (b,c) has a finite QP value exactly when the feasible set is nonempty and every triple (x,v,η) satisfying feasibility, stationarity, and complementarity also satisfies (c+Qx)ᵀv ≥ 0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (b,c)\in\operatorname{dom}(Q,A)\iff\left[\mathcal P_A(b)\ne\varnothing\ \land\ \forall(x,v,\eta),\ \bigl(Qv-A^\top\eta=0,\ 0\le\eta\perp Av\ge0,\ Ax\ge b\bigr)\Rightarrow(c+Qx)^\top v\ge0\right].

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Marginal Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity under partial minimization in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(v:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(v(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\). If \(F\) is jointly convex, then \(v\) is convex in the extended-valued sense: for all \(x_1,x_2\in X\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[v(tx_1+(1-t)x_2)\leq tv(x_1)+(1-t)v(x_2).\] Partial minimization does not by itself guarantee lower semicontinuity, attainment, or differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partially minimizing a jointly convex function preserves convexity, but the resulting marginal function need not be lower semicontinuous, attained, or differentiable.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(F:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The marginal function \(v(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\) is convex, although it need not be differentiable or closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Lower-Solution Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete bilevel response ambiguity caused by two lower minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the lower problem \(\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}}(y^2-1)^2\), whose solution mapping is \(M(x)=\{-1,1\}\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). With \(H(x,y)=xy\), the responses \(y=1\) and \(y=-1\) yield \(x\) and \(-x\), respectively, so lower optimality does not determine a single response value. Under the optimistic convention, \[\varphi(x)=\min_{y\in M(x)}xy=\min\{x,-x\}=-|x|,\] whereas the pessimistic value is \(|x|\). Both values are nondifferentiable at \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two equally optimal lower responses produce different upper objectives; optimistic and pessimistic conventions yield minus absolute value and absolute value, both nonsmooth at zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Lower-solution nonuniqueness makes response substitution ambiguous and produces the optimistic value \(-|x|\), which is nondifferentiable at \(0\).

children.title: Worst-Case Adversarial Value Family
children.top_down_role: Worst-case and adversarial response models that induce max-value or marginal objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Scenario Worst-Case Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite adversarial scenario maximum and simplex representation for real-valued scenario losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) and let \(f_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) for every \(i\in I\). The finite-scenario worst-case objective is \[F(x)=\max_{i\in I}f_i(x)=\max_{p\in\Delta_N}\sum_{i=1}^N p_i f_i(x),\qquad \Delta_N=\{p\in\mathbb{R}_+^N:\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}p=1\}.\] Its active scenario set is \(I(x)=\{i\in I:f_i(x)=F(x)\}\), which is nonempty. If all \(f_i\) are differentiable, ties between active scenarios with unequal gradients can make \(F\) nondifferentiable. If all \(f_i\) are convex, then \(F\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-scenario worst-case model is the maximum of real-valued scenario losses, equivalently the maximum expected loss over the probability simplex; active-scenario ties can create nonsmoothness.
assumptions_latex: \(I=\{1,\ldots,N\}\) is a nonempty finite scenario set.
Each \(f_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is a real-valued scenario loss.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case loss is \(F(x)=\max_{i\in I}f_i(x)\), equivalently the simplex maximum, and active scenarios attain this value.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncertainty-Set Value Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic worst-case value induced by a prescribed uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a decision set, let \(U\neq\varnothing\) be an uncertainty set, and let \(\ell:X\times U\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a loss function. The uncertainty-set value model is
\[V(x):=\sup_{u\in U}\ell(x,u),\qquad x\in X.\]
Thus the robust optimization problem \(\inf_{x\in X}V(x)\) is equivalent to \(\inf\{t:(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R,\ \ell(x,u)\le t\ \text{for every }u\in U\}\). Even when every function \(\ell(\cdot,u)\) is smooth, the supremum can be nonsmooth where multiple uncertainty realizations attain the worst-case value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A robust value is the largest loss over the uncertainty set; minimizing it is equivalent to imposing one epigraph inequality for every uncertainty realization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(x)=\sup_{u\in U}\ell(x,u)\)

notation.meaning: loss at decision x and realization u

knowledge_statements.title: Distributionally Robust Value Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case expected loss over an ambiguity set of probability laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\) be a measurable space, let \(X\) be a decision set, and let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty collection of probability measures on \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\). For a measurable loss \(\ell:X\times\Xi\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) whose expectation is well defined for every \(P\in\mathcal P\), the distributionally robust value is
\[V(x):=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[\ell(x,\xi)].\]
The associated model minimizes \(V\) over \(X\). Nonsmoothness may arise when the maximizing distribution changes or several distributions attain the supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distributionally robust model minimizes the largest expected loss among all probability laws in a prescribed ambiguity set.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell(x,\cdot)\) is measurable and has a well-defined expectation for every \(x\in X\) and \(P\in\mathcal P\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(x)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[\ell(x,\xi)]\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimistic–Pessimistic Probability-Ambiguity Value Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample value model combining favorable and adverse probability reweightings of sample losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y_s(x)=\varphi(m(x,\xi^s);z_s)\), let \(w_{\mathrm o},w_{\mathrm p}>0\), let \(\Delta_{\mathrm o},\Delta_{\mathrm p}\) be closed convex sets of discrete probability vectors, and let \(c_{\mathrm o},c_{\mathrm p}\) be nonnegative cost functions. Define
\[
v_{\mathrm{op}}^{\mathrm{pr}}(x)=w_{\mathrm o}\min_{p^{\mathrm o}\in\Delta_{\mathrm o}}\left\{(p^{\mathrm o})^Ty(x)+c_{\mathrm o}(p^{\mathrm o})\right\}+w_{\mathrm p}\max_{p^{\mathrm p}\in\Delta_{\mathrm p}}\left\{(p^{\mathrm p})^Ty(x)-c_{\mathrm p}(p^{\mathrm p})\right\}.
\]
The optimistic and pessimistic probability optimizations are separable. If both ambiguity sets are the singleton containing the uniform empirical probability vector and both costs vanish there, this value reduces to the empirical average loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value combines an optimistic minimum and a pessimistic maximum over probability reweightings of the sample losses. These two inner optimizations separate. Restricting both ambiguity sets to the uniform empirical distribution and using zero costs recovers empirical risk minimization.
assumptions_latex: \Delta_{\mathrm o},\Delta_{\mathrm p}\subseteq\{p\in\mathbb R_+^N:\mathbf 1^Tp=1\}\text{ are closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v_{\mathrm{op}}^{\mathrm{pr}}(x)=w_{\mathrm o}\min_{p^{\mathrm o}\in\Delta_{\mathrm o}}\{(p^{\mathrm o})^Ty(x)+c_{\mathrm o}(p^{\mathrm o})\}+w_{\mathrm p}\max_{p^{\mathrm p}\in\Delta_{\mathrm p}}\{(p^{\mathrm p})^Ty(x)-c_{\mathrm p}(p^{\mathrm p})\}

children.title: Interdiction Models
children.top_down_role: Leader interventions that alter a subordinate system or feasible response.

knowledge_statements.title: Interdiction Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential attack followed by an optimizing defender response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\) be the feasible interdiction set and let \(Y(a)\neq\varnothing\) be the defender's feasible response set after attack \(a\in A\). Given an attacker payoff \(L(a,y)\), define the defender-response value
\[q(a):=\inf_{y\in Y(a)}L(a,y).\]
A max-min interdiction model is
\[\sup_{a\in A}q(a)=\sup_{a\in A}\inf_{y\in Y(a)}L(a,y).\]
The value function \(q\) may be nonsmooth when the optimal defender response changes, and it may be discontinuous when the response mapping \(Y\) lacks suitable stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attacker selects an interdiction action, after which the defender optimally responds; the attacker maximizes the resulting response value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{a\in A}q(a)=\sup_{a\in A}\inf_{y\in Y(a)}L(a,y)\)

notation.meaning: defender response set after attack a

children.title: Adversarial Response Models
children.top_down_role: Objectives induced by an optimizing opponent or hostile responder.

knowledge_statements.title: Adversarial Response Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value model generated by an adversary's optimal response correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a decision set, let \(U(x)\neq\varnothing\) be the adversary's feasible-response set, and let \(L:X\times U\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be the modeled loss. The adversarial response correspondence and induced value function are
\[R(x):=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{u\in U(x)}L(x,u),\qquad V(x):=\sup_{u\in U(x)}L(x,u).\]
Whenever the maximum is attained, every \(u\in R(x)\) satisfies \(V(x)=L(x,u)\). Changes in the active response set \(R(x)\) are a primary source of nonsmoothness of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The adversary chooses a feasible response maximizing loss; the optimized response value can become nonsmooth when the active response changes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V(x)=\sup_{u\in U(x)}L(x,u)\)

children.title: Attacker-Defender Value Structures
children.top_down_role: Nested value constructions coupling disruptive choices with defensive recourse.

knowledge_statements.title: Attacker-Defender Value Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stackelberg value with an attacker moving before a minimizing defender.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\) be the attack set, let \(D(a)\neq\varnothing\) be the defender's feasible set after \(a\in A\), and let \(L(a,d)\) denote the attacker's payoff. The defender value and attacker-defender value are
\[q(a):=\inf_{d\in D(a)}L(a,d),\qquad V:=\sup_{a\in A}q(a).\]
If both extrema are attained, a pair \((a^*,d^*)\) realizes this sequential value when \(d^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{d\in D(a^*)}L(a^*,d)\) and \(a^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in A}q(a)\). This sequential value need not equal the reversed min-max value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The defender minimizes payoff after observing the attack, and the attacker chooses an action maximizing that optimized defender-response value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V=\sup_{a\in A}\inf_{d\in D(a)}L(a,d)\)

notation.meaning: defender feasible set following attack a

children.title: Stochastic Nonsmooth Models

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation-Function Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected integrand as a deterministic stochastic-programming objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Xi,\mathcal A,P)\) be a probability space, let \(X\) be a decision set, and let \(h:X\times\Xi\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be measurable in its second argument. At every \(x\in X\) for which the expectation is well defined, the expectation function is
\[F(x):=\mathbb E_P[h(x,\xi)]=\int_{\Xi}h(x,z)\,P(dz).\]
An expectation-function model minimizes \(F\) over \(X\), possibly with additional deterministic constraints. Nonsmoothness of \(F\) can be inherited from \(h(\cdot,z)\), even when integration averages over the random outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expectation-function model optimizes the probability-weighted average of a measurable random integrand over the decision set.
assumptions_latex: \(h(x,\cdot)\) is measurable and its expectation is well defined on the stated domain
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=\mathbb E_P[h(x,\xi)]\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits expectation-function models and introduces the probability space, integrand, and domain. No inspectable source is cited for the model or the nonsmoothness statement, so the record remains source-dependent.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Average Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample empirical approximation of an expectation-function objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given observations \(\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^N\) and an integrand \(h:X\times\Xi\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), the sample-average approximation of \(F(x)=\mathbb E[h(x,\xi)]\) is
\[F_N(x):=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}h(x,\xi^j),\qquad x\in X.\]
The sample-average model is \(\inf_{x\in X}F_N(x)\), together with any sampled or deterministic constraints specified by the underlying stochastic program. For a fixed sample, \(F_N\) is a finite-sum nonsmooth objective whenever one or more sampled functions \(h(\cdot,\xi^j)\) are nonsmooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sample-average model replaces an expectation by the arithmetic mean of losses evaluated at finitely many sampled outcomes.
assumptions_latex: \(h(x,\xi^j)\) is defined for every \(x\in X\) and \(j=1,\ldots,N\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-sum definition fits the sample-average-model leaf. However, the observations are not explicitly characterized as a random sample, independent sample, or fixed empirical data, and no source is provided to determine the intended sample-average convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Stage Recourse Value Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected optimal second-stage value induced by a first-stage decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be the first-stage feasible set. For outcome \(\xi\), let \(Y(x,\xi)\neq\varnothing\) be the feasible recourse set and let \(q(x,y,\xi)\) be the second-stage cost. Define
\[Q(x,\xi):=\inf_{y\in Y(x,\xi)}q(x,y,\xi),\qquad F(x):=c(x)+\mathbb E[Q(x,\xi)].\]
The two-stage recourse model is \(\inf_{x\in X}F(x)\), provided the expectation is well defined. The value \(Q(\cdot,\xi)\) can be nonsmooth when the optimal recourse solution or active constraints change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-stage decision incurs immediate cost plus the expected optimal cost of adapting through a feasible second-stage response.
assumptions_latex: \(Q(x,\xi)\) is measurable in \(\xi\) and has a well-defined expectation
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=c(x)+\mathbb E[\inf_{y\in Y(x,\xi)}q(x,y,\xi)]\)
